name: Scottie Pippen
description: Scottie Pippen (born September 25, 1965, in Hamburg, Arkansas, the youngest of twelve children) is the forward who, alongside Michael Jordan, turned the Chicago Bulls into the defining team of the 1990s. Overlooked by major college programs, he walked on at the University of Central Arkansas, was drafted fifth overall in 1987 by Seattle, and was traded to Chicago on draft night. Across seventeen NBA seasons — twelve with the Bulls — he won six NBA championships (1991–1993, 1996–1998), seven All-Star selections, eight All-Defensive First Team honors, and the 1994 All-Star Game MVP award. He is the only player to win an NBA championship and an Olympic gold medal in the same year twice (1992 and 1996, the first with the original Dream Team). Chicago retired his No. 33 in 2005, and he entered the Basketball Hall of Fame in 2010, both individually and as a member of the Dream Team.

name: Songs in the Key of Life
description: Songs in the Key of Life is the 1976 double album by Stevie Wonder, released by Motown's Tamla label on September 28, 1976, with a four-song bonus EP, A Something's Extra. Written, arranged, produced and largely performed by Wonder at the summit of his classic period, it carries “Sir Duke,” his tribute to the jazz masters; “I Wish”; “Isn't She Lovely”; and “As.” The album debuted at number one on the Billboard 200 and won the Grammy Award for Album of the Year — Wonder's third such award — at the 1977 Grammy ceremony. It was certified Diamond by the RIAA, inducted into the Grammy Hall of Fame in 2002, and added to the Library of Congress's National Recording Registry in 2005. Rolling Stone ranked it fourth on its 2020 revision of the 500 greatest albums of all time.

name: Sepia
description: Sepia was a photojournalistic magazine of Black achievement and everyday life, founded in Fort Worth, Texas, in 1946 as Negro Achievements by Horace J. Blackwell, an African American clothing merchant. Published by the Good Publishing Company (ISSN 0037-2374), it was edited from its founding years by a team in which women held leading roles, including editorial director Adelle Martin Jackson and Beatrice Pringle. After Blackwell's death in 1948, George Levitan bought the company in 1950 and renamed the magazine in stages — Sepia Record in 1953, then Sepia in 1954. It serialized John Howard Griffin's undercover reporting that became Black Like Me, covered civil-rights struggle and Black institutions for a national audience, and stood for nearly four decades as Ebony's most durable competitor. Levitan published it until his death in 1976; Pringle then bought the magazine and ran it until its final issue in 1983, at a reported circulation near 160,000. Its photographic files survive at the African American Museum in Dallas.

description: Summer of Soul (...Or, When the Revolution Could Not Be Televised) is a 2021 American documentary film about the 1969 Harlem Cultural Festival, directed by Ahmir 'Questlove' Thompson in his directorial debut. The festival took place on six Sundays between June 29 and August 24, 1969, at Mount Morris Park in Harlem, and television producer Hal Tulchin recorded about 40 hours of footage at the request of festival organizer Tony Lawrence. Apart from two one-hour television specials broadcast in 1969, the tapes then sat in a basement for the next 50 years. The film interweaves the restored festival footage with stock news footage and modern interviews, presenting performances by Stevie Wonder, Mahalia Jackson, Nina Simone, The 5th Dimension, The Staple Singers, Gladys Knight and the Pips, Sly and the Family Stone and others. It premiered on January 28, 2021, at the Sundance Film Festival, where it won the Grand Jury Prize and the Audience Award in the documentary categories, and was released by Searchlight Pictures and Hulu in June 2021. It won Best Documentary Feature at the 94th Academy Awards and Best Music Film at the 64th Grammy Awards.

name: Sanford and Son
description: Sanford and Son, developed by Norman Lear and Bud Yorkin from the BBC's Steptoe and Son, aired on NBC from January 14, 1972, to March 25, 1977 — six seasons, 136 episodes built on Redd Foxx as Fred Sanford, a Watts junk dealer whose theatrical heart attacks ('This is the big one!') were aimed at his son Lamont, played by Demond Wilson. Its theme was composed by Quincy Jones. The ratings were emphatic: the series finished in the Nielsen top ten in five of its six seasons, peaking at No. 2, and Time placed it on its All-TIME 100 TV Shows list in 2007. Hailed as NBC's answer to All in the Family and as the precursor to the Black sitcoms that followed, it established the form's essential proof a decade before the Huxtables: a Black comic persona, drawn from the Chitlin' Circuit stage, could hold a network's Friday night against anything. For this graph, Sanford is the shelf's foundation stone — the first of the Lear-era records and the one from which Good Times and The Jeffersons descend in television's own family tree.

description: Seun Kuti (born Oluseun Anikulapo Kuti on January 11, 1983, in Lagos, Nigeria) is the Nigerian saxophonist and singer who is the youngest son of Afrobeat creator Fela Kuti (CTL-E-5697) and the brother of Femi Kuti. name: Sterling Plumpp
description: Sterling Plumpp (born January 30, 1940, in Clinton, Mississippi) is a Chicago blues poet whose work builds poems out of the rhythms, structures, and personae of the blues and jazz. Raised by sharecropper grandparents in Mississippi, he hitchhiked to Chicago in 1962, worked in the main post office, and earned a B.A. (1968) and M.A. (1971) from Roosevelt University. His first poems appeared in Negro Digest in 1971, the year he joined the University of Illinois at Chicago, where he taught English and African American studies for thirty years before retiring as professor emeritus in 2001. He is the author of fourteen books, including The Mojo Hands Call, I Must Go, Blues: The Story Always Untold, Velvet BeBop Kente Cloth, and Home/Bass (Third World Press, 2013), written out of his friendship and songwriting work with Chicago blues bassist Willie Kent. His honors include the Carl Sandburg Literary Award, the Richard Wright Literary Excellence Award, an American Book Award for Home/Bass, and the Chicago Literary Hall of Fame's Fuller Award for lifetime achievement in 2019.

name: Syl Johnson
description: Syl Johnson, born Sylvester Thompson in Mississippi on July 1, 1936, came to Chicago with his family around 1950 and grew up next door to blues guitarist Magic Sam, playing in the 1950s alongside Sam, Billy Boy Arnold, Junior Wells, and Howlin' Wolf. He made his solo recording debut in 1959 and, after lean years, became the star of Chicago's Twinight Records. His 1967 Different Strokes and his 1969 Is It Because I'm Black, written in the aftermath of Martin Luther King Jr.'s assassination, defined his two legacies: the first became one of the most sampled recordings in hip-hop, borrowed by Wu-Tang Clan, Public Enemy, De La Soul, and many others, while the second stands among the most direct civil-rights statements in soul music. In the 1970s he recorded for Hi Records in Memphis, including his 1975 version of Take Me to the River. Johnson pursued sampling royalties assertively and successfully, and archival reissues restored his catalog to view. He died on February 6, 2022, aged 85, weeks after his brother, bluesman Jimmy Johnson.

name: Snowfall
description: Snowfall, created by John Singleton, Eric Amadio, and Dave Andron — Andron serving as showrunner — aired on FX from July 5, 2017, to April 19, 2023: six seasons, sixty episodes that began as a 2014 Showtime project before FX picked it up. Set at the onset of the crack epidemic in 1980s South Central Los Angeles, it braided three storylines — a young dealer, Franklin Saint, building an empire; a CIA operative moving money and cocaine toward the Nicaraguan Contras; and the cartel families supplying both — making federal complicity a structural element of the plot rather than a background suggestion. Its premiere ranked among the top five new cable drama premieres of 2017 in key demographics. It was Singleton's final major television work: production of the third season continued after his death in 2019, and the series ran six years as his sustained argument that the epidemic was a policy outcome with authors, not a weather event. The graph files Snowfall as the prestige shelf's reckoning with the crack era — the dramatic counterpart to the documentary record, told by the filmmaker who had opened the hood-film era a generation earlier.

name: Shonda Rhimes
description: Shonda Rhimes, born Shonda Lynn Rhimes on January 13, 1970, in Chicago, Illinois, is an American television producer, screenwriter, and author, the youngest of six children, raised in Park Forest South (now University Park). She attended Marian Catholic High School in Chicago Heights, earned a B.A. in English and film studies from Dartmouth College in 1991, and an M.F.A. from the USC School of Cinematic Arts, where she received the Gary Rosenberg Writing Fellowship. After working as research director on the documentary Hank Aaron: Chasing the Dream (1995), she wrote the HBO film Introducing Dorothy Dandridge (1999) and the features Crossroads (2002) and The Princess Diaries 2 (2004). She founded the production company Shondaland and created Grey's Anatomy (2005), Private Practice (2007), and Scandal (2012), becoming the first African American woman to create three television series that each passed 100 episodes. In 2017 she signed a major overall deal with Netflix, where Shondaland produced Bridgerton (2020) and Inventing Anna (2022). She was inducted into the Television Hall of Fame in 2017 and published the memoir Year of Yes in 2015.

name: Savoy Ballroom
description: The Savoy Ballroom was a Bronzeville dance hall at 4733 S. Parkway (now Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. Drive), at 47th Street, celebrated in the graph record as the "World's Finest Ballroom" for Black dancers. It opened in November 1927 as part of a single commercial complex with the Regal Theater and the South Center Department Store, developed by a syndicate headed by Harry M. and Louis Englestein and operated by dance promoter I. Jay Faggen; the complex helped make 47th Street's reputation as the "Harlem of Chicago." The ballroom accommodated more than 4,000 people and anchored the 47th and South Parkway bright-light district. University of Chicago exhibit research treats it as a major jazz center, and CTL's corridor research dates its era from the late 1920s to its closing in 1954, with demolition in the early 1970s; the site is now occupied by the Harold Washington Cultural Center. Corpus sources dispute the exact end dates, and this record flags that dispute rather than smoothing it.

name: Supreme Life Insurance Company
description: The Supreme Life Insurance Company was a historic Black-owned Chicago insurer founded in 1919 by Frank L. Gillespie, an Arkansas native and agent for the Royal Insurance Company, as the Liberty Life Insurance Company — the first Black-owned and operated insurance company in the northern United States — and later renamed Supreme Life. Its headquarters building at 3501 S. King Drive was built in 1921 (architect Albert Anis), purchased by the company in 1924, and served as its headquarters into 1962. In 1929 the company merged with two other Black firms in a combination reported at $27 million. The young John H. Johnson worked as an office clerk at Supreme Life before founding Johnson Publishing, making the insurer a literal training ground for Black Chicago's publishing empire. The company is the subject of Robert C. Puth's Business History Review study, the first scholarly study of an individual Black life insurance firm. Its building — saved from near-demolition in the 1990s, rehabilitated in 2005, and now the Bronzeville Visitor Information Center — is one of the nine Black Metropolis structures designated Chicago Landmarks on September 9, 1998. The company's fate after 1962 is unresolved in CTL's corpus, so the record's "contemporary" era framing is not asserted here.

description: Clifton Dillon created the Solid Gold sound system in Chicago after relocating there.

name: Sakad
description: Evanston-based Haitian band; performed at Northwestern University's fourth annual CaribFest (May 2003) alongside DJ Sagittarius.

name: São Paulo, Brazil
description: Brazilian city where Katherine Dunham's July 1950 hotel-discrimination episode catalyzed Brazil's first anti-racial-prejudice law; also the Brazilian legislative party to a declared sister-city relationship with Chicago.

name: Segundo Ruiz Belvis Cultural Center
description: Chicago's longest-running Latino/Latine cultural center (est. 1971), emphasizing African heritage in Puerto Rican and Latin American arts.

name: Sunset Café
description: Landmarked integrated ('Black and Tan') jazz club in a converted 1909 auto garage; hosted Louis Armstrong, Earl Hines, and Cab Calloway. Distinct venue from the Grand Terrace Cafe despite frequent online conflation.

name: Sam Chatman
description: DJ/promoter Sam Chatman, known as the 'Godfather of Steppin',' coined the name 'Stepping' for the Chicago partner dance in 1974 after announcing at a party that a dancing couple looked like they were 'stepping.'

name: Sonny Thompson
description: Organist Sonny Thompson played in the regular band of Chess session musicians on Chicago soul recordings.

name: Stu Black
description: Engineer Stu Black recorded early AACM avant-garde jazz at Hall Studios and later Sound Studios (230 N. Michigan Ave), engineering Roscoe Mitchell's 'Sound' (Delmark, 1966).

name: Shawn Christopher
description: Chicago dance-music singer; touring backing vocalist for Chaka Khan (1982-1985); voice of the 1986 D.J. International house single 'People Of All Nations'; 1990s Arista dance hits 'Another Sleepless Night' (1991) and 'Don't Lose the Magic' (1992), both Billboard Hot Dance Club Play No. 1s; sang on Lil' Louis's 'French Kiss'.

name: Smashed Plastic
description: Smashed Plastic is a Chicago vinyl record pressing plant in the former Hammond Organ factory on Chicago's North Side, described in its research package as the city's first vinyl pressing plant in decades. It was founded by Andy Weber, John Lombardo, and Steve Polutnik, and presses records for local musicians and labels. The graph dates the business from 2018, and its opening was reported in 2019 by WBBM Newsradio and Chicago Talks, with Resident Advisor describing it as Chicago's first vinyl pressing plant in two decades. In CTL's music-infrastructure research it represents the return of record manufacturing itself to Chicago, after decades in which local artists' vinyl was pressed elsewhere.

name: Soul Train archive (television)
description: Soul Train began in Chicago in 1970 on WCIU-TV before moving to Los Angeles in 1971; its archive is the definitive televisual record of Black popular music performance. The show's Chicago roots — Don Cornelius's WVON background — tie it directly to the constellation's radio node.

name: Satellite radio Black channels
aliases: SiriusXM Black channels; SiriusXM Urban & Caribbean
description: SiriusXM's dedicated Black/urban channel lineup, grouped under its 'Urban & Caribbean' category: Rock the Bells Radio (43), Hip-Hop Nation (44), Shade 45 (45), The Heat (46), Heart & Soul (47), The Flow (48), SiriusXM FLY (50), The Groove (51), Smokey's Soul Town (74), plus gospel via Kirk Franklin's Praise (64) and app-only extensions. Black-formatted, corporate-owned.

name: Say Brother / Basic Black
description: Longest-running Black public-affairs TV program on WGBH Boston (1968–2024): Say Brother (1968–1997), premiered July 1968 three months after MLK's assassination; retitled Basic Black in 1998 by producer Cynthia Johnson. Aired weekly documentaries, performances, and conversations with guests from Muhammad Ali to Maya Angelou; AAPB holds ~1,000 episodes/segments. WGBH ended it as a TV production in May 2024; succeeded by GBH News Rooted (host Paris Alston, 2025).

name: Scott Mills
description: BET Media Group president (January 2018) and CEO (2021–December 2025). Joined BET in 1997 as SVP of business development (ex-Lehman Brothers; ex-Deputy Treasurer of Philadelphia); held president, COO, CFO, and president of digital media roles; launched BET Mobile, BET.com, and the Centric channel; Viacom chief administrative officer 2012–2018. Oversaw the BET+ launch (Sept 19, 2019, with Tyler Perry Studios) and the creation of BET Studios (2021). Exited after 23 years following the Skydance merger; succeeded by Louis Carr.

name: Service Broadcasting
aliases: Service Broadcasting Corporation; Service Broadcasting Group; SBG
description: Dallas radio operator of Black-format stations KKDA-FM ('K104') and KRNB ('Smooth R&B 105.7'), founded/owned by Hymen Childs (acquired KKDA 1976; signed on KRNB 1996). Sold KKDA-AM in 2013; agreed May 2026 to sell KKDA-FM and KRNB to Urban One (Radio One) in a reported $22M deal. CORRECTION 2026-10-06: not Black-owned - D Magazine identified owner Hymen Childs as white and Jewish (conflict CTL-CFL-002583).

name: Sheridan Broadcasting Corporation
description: Pittsburgh-based Black-owned broadcast company founded 1972 by Ronald and Judith Davenport; first Black-owned radio network in the U.S. Bought 49% of the Mutual Black Network (1976) and the rest (1979), renaming it the Sheridan Broadcasting Network; SBN merged with the National Black Network in 1991 to form American Urban Radio Networks (51% owner until forced out in 2016); later went out of business.

name: Sherrell Dorsey
description: Data journalist, entrepreneur, speaker, and author; founder of The Plug, the first daily Black tech newsletter (April 2016), later a data-driven tech news platform syndicated on the Bloomberg Terminal and acquired by ImpactAlpha; author of 'Upper Hand: The Future of Work for the Rest of Us' (Wiley); Columbia data-journalism master's; Northwestern Medill/Garage entrepreneur-in-residence.

name: Soul Train media library
description: The Soul Train media library is the television archive of Soul Train: more than 1,100 episodes and 40 specials from the 1970s through the first decade of the 2000s, described by BET as 'one of the largest libraries of African American music-oriented content in the world.' Don Cornelius sold Soul Train to InterMedia Partners in 2008; in April 2016 BET, under Viacom, acquired the brand and library from InterMedia Partners and the Yucaipa Companies, in a deal that closed on April 4, 2016. BET president Debra Lee framed the acquisition explicitly as a commercial intellectual-property strategy built on licensing, live events, and consumer products. The library's survival therefore followed a corporate-consolidation model — preserved as commercial IP through acquisition rather than through a public archive, with no public archival access program described in the deal's record.

name: St. Louis American
description: The St. Louis American is a St. Louis weekly founded in 1928 — the city's only continuously published Black newspaper — first issued March 17, 1928, as a paid tabloid with circulation over 2,000; the founding is generally credited to Judge Nathan B. Young Jr. and Black businessmen including Homer G. Phillips. Nathaniel Sweets joined in 1928, became publisher in 1933, and owned the paper for 45+ years, until 1981. In 1981 Donald Suggs and two investors bought majority shares; Suggs became majority stockholder and publisher in 1984, converting it from a limited paid weekly (about 4,400 circulation) to a free one. It reports distributing 70,000+ copies free at 845+ locations each Thursday and claims to have been Missouri's largest weekly since 2012 — a self-reported claim flagged as needing citation.

name: Shorefront Legacy Center
description: Community archive in Evanston, Illinois, founded 1995 by Dino Robinson and run by Laurice Bell from the basement of the Lula B. Sherman Church; documents 100+ years of Black life on Chicago's North Shore (NAACP minutes, segregation correspondence). Its records underpinned the report behind Evanston's apology and first-in-the-nation cash reparations program ($25,000 per person); residents used it to prove 1919-1969 residency in 2021.

name: Stony Island Arts Bank Collections
description: Theaster Gates's Rebuild Foundation stewardship of four Black-focused collections in a rescued 1923 bank building (purchased from the city for $1; reopened 2015): the JPC reference library (12,000-15,000+ vols.), Frankie Knuckles's vinyl, the Edward J. Williams "negrobilia" collection (~4,000 artifacts), 60,000+ UChicago glass lantern slides.

name: Separate Cinema Archive
description: John Duke Kisch's 37,000-item private collection of African American film memorabilia (1904–2019): original posters, stills, publicity material, scripts, lobby cards, and a reference library — named for the 'race films' era and called the most prominent African American film history repository. Collected over ~40 years; housed in Poughkeepsie, New York. Acquired by the Lucas Museum of Narrative Art (announced January 2020; prior stub date 2025-01 corrected, see CTL-CFL-002566).

name: Sherry Williams
description: Founder and president of the Bronzeville Historical Society (1999); Englewood-raised, first generation of her family born in Chicago; videotaped 11 years of oral histories of Bronzeville residents' Great Migration journeys (digitized 2009); Quinn Chapel AME member; 2012 Audubon Fellow; author of '100 Notable People and Places in Bronzeville.'

name: Separate Cinema Archive acquired by Lucas Museum
description: (2020-01-15) The Lucas Museum of Narrative Art's acquisition of John Duke Kisch's 37,000-item Separate Cinema Archive, announced January 2020 (Smithsonian, Jan 16; Bard, Jan 19) — CORRECTED from the prior stub date of 2025-01 (see CTL-CFL-002566). Marked with Black History Month screenings (The Wiz, Do the Right Thing) on Feb 8, 2020 at Baldwin Hills Crenshaw Plaza with LACMA. The museum, founded by George Lucas and Mellody Hobson in Exposition Park, Los Angeles, set a September 2026 opening.

name: South Center Department Store
description: Department store in the Englestein-developed 47th/S. Parkway complex. Open/close dates, ownership, and fate unresolved.

name: States Theater
description: 700-seat Black theater at the Panama (3501) / De Luxe Cafe (3503) / States corner cluster; described as one of the most prominent Black theaters in Chicago's Black Belt.

name: Supreme Life / Liberty Life Insurance Company Building
description: Headquarters of the first Black-owned insurance company in the northern United States (founded 1919 by Frank L. Gillespie); saved from near-demolition in the 1990s; now the Bronzeville Visitor Information Center.

name: St. Mark Methodist Episcopal Church (now St. Mark United Methodist)
description: Established 1893 in a State Street storefront; a documented example of the storefront-church phenomenon.

name: St. Clair Drake / Horace R. Cayton
description: Authors of 'Black Metropolis' (1945); codified the 'city within a city' thesis. Treat as scholarship, not scripture.

name: Southtown Theatre
description: Rapp & Rapp South Side movie palace; theater-to-retail conversion

name: Stratford Theatre
description: Warner Bros. neighborhood theater at 715 W. 63rd St, Englewood. Opened September 4, 1920, with 2,433 seats and a Moller 3-manual 22-rank organ; built for Cooney Brothers National Theaters Corp. Often said to be where Bob Hope got his first start. Torn down.

name: Stage Lounge
description: Chuck Berry, Art Blakey bookings in the 1950s

name: Strand Show Lounge
description: Strand Hotel show lounge

name: Sears, Roebuck & Co. (Englewood)
description: Seven-story, 290,000-sq-ft Sears department store at 63rd & Halsted, Englewood. Opened 1934 (construction date disputed: 1929 vs 1934). Anchor of the 63rd/Halsted shopping district; closed January 1976; later demolished.

name: Shrine of Christ the King
aliases: Shrine of Christ the King Sovereign Priest; St. Clara; St. Clara–St. Cyril; St. Gelasius
description: Roman Catholic shrine at 6401 S. Woodlawn Ave., Woodlawn, now administered by the Institute of Christ the King Sovereign Priest. Founded as St. Clara parish (1894); Renaissance Revival church by Henry J. Schlacks finished 1928; renamed St. Clara–St. Cyril (1969) and St. Gelasius (1990); closed 2002; designated a Chicago Landmark January 14, 2004; damaged by fires in 1976 and 2015.

name: St. Rita of Cascia Parish
description: Roman Catholic (Augustinian) parish at 6243 S. Fairfield Ave., Chicago Lawn, founded 1905 — described as the first Augustinian church in Chicago. United with St. Clare of Montefalco Parish effective July 1, 2020 under Renew My Church; serves a primarily Latino community. Associated St. Rita of Cascia High School (all-boys, founded 1905) remains in operation.

name: St. Benedict the African Parish (Roman Catholic)
description: Roman Catholic parish at 340 W. 66th St., Englewood, formed from the merger of eight parishes as the neighborhood became predominantly African-American; two worship sites became separate parishes in 1995 and re-merged in 2016. Distinctive African-hut-inspired architecture; included in Chicago Architecture Foundation Open House Chicago.

name: St. John EMBC Church
description: St. John EMBC Church is located at 1234 W.

name: St. Mary's M.B. Church
description: St. Mary's Missionary Baptist Church is located at 1040 W.

name: St. Rita of Cascia High School
description: St. Rita of Cascia High School is an all-boys Catholic high school in Chicago, founded in 1905 by Very Rev. James F. Green, O.S.A. Its campus is at 7740 S. Western Ave. The school's centennial was recognized in the Congressional Record on July 27, 2005, in remarks entered by Rep. Daniel Lipinski marking the founding. The school is a historically related institution of St. Rita of Cascia Parish, the Augustinian parish at 63rd Street and Fairfield Avenue in Chicago Lawn, founded in 1905 as the first Augustinian church in Chicago.

name: Southwest Organizing Project (SWOP) Reclaiming Project
description: Southwest Organizing Project initiative in a 20-square-block area around St. Rita of Cascia (63rd & Fairfield). Began June 2012 with 93 vacant buildings; by 2019 only 8 remained vacant and 85 had been converted to affordable housing. Partners include United Power for Action and Justice; praised by Cardinal Cupich.

name: Save A Lot Englewood
description: Save A Lot grocery store at 832 W. 63rd St., Englewood, in the former Whole Foods building; opened May 11, 2023, operated by the Black-owned platform Yellow Banana (127 Wall Holdings) amid community opposition over food quality and engagement, after an April opening was postponed by protest. Backed by $13.5M in city TIF money. Closed July 25, 2026 with six other Chicago stores after Save A Lot ended its Yellow Banana arrangement.

name: Sarah E. Goode
aliases: Sarah Elisabeth Jacobs; Sarah Elizabeth Jacobs
description: Chicago inventor and entrepreneur; granted U.S. patent 322,177 on July 14, 1885 for a folding cabinet bed, making her one of the first African American women to receive a U.S. patent. Born Sarah Elisabeth Jacobs about 1855 in Toledo, Ohio; moved to Chicago before 1870; married carpenter Archibald Goode. The cabinet bed folded into a desk with storage compartments, designed for small urban apartments. Died in Chicago, April 8, 1905. TYPE CORRECTED Institution->Person (RELP111).

name: Sylvester Johnson
description: Northwestern University professor of Black Studies whose listed focus areas include AI, data bias, discrimination, human-machine interaction, and inequality.

name: South Street Journal
description: South Side community paper founded by Ron Carter

name: Simeon Booker
description: Trailblazing Black journalist; first full-time Black reporter at The Washington Post (1952-1954); Jet/Ebony Washington bureau chief for 51 years (retired 2007); covered the 1955 Emmett Till murder and trial; only journalist to ride with the first Freedom Riders (1961); first Black winner of the National Press Club Fourth Estate Award (1982); author of 'Shocking the Conscience' (2013) and 'Black Man's America' (1964); died 2017-12-10 in Solomons, MD, age 99.

name: Savoy Big Five
description: Black basketball team providing paid pre-dance exhibition entertainment at Chicago's Savoy Ballroom on the South Side. Originated in 1926 when former Wendell Phillips High School players reunited as the Giles Post American Legion team; took the Savoy Big Five name in 1927 while playing home games at the newly opened Savoy Ballroom. From January 1928 the exhibitions propped up the ballroom's declining dance attendance. In late 1928 a pay dispute led players to bolt and form the barnstorming "Globe Trotters"; promoter Abe Saperstein re-christened them the "New York Harlem Globe Trotters" -- the team that became the Harlem Globetrotters.

name: South Shore Commission
description: Community conservation organization that managed South Shore's racial transition through 'managed integration' - included here as a counter-institution: an organization Black residents lived under but did not control Geography: Chicago, Illinois (South Shore)

name: St. Bernard Hospital and Health Care Center
description: Independent Catholic safety-net hospital founded 1904 in Englewood; the last remaining community hospital in its neighborhood, serving a patient base over 90% Medicaid/Medicare.

name: St. Elizabeth Catholic School
description: Bronzeville Catholic grade school at 4052 S. Wabash: successor of the merger of St. Elizabeth parish (founded 1881 for Irish Catholics) with St. Monica (founded 1893/1894 by Augustus Tolton, the Black parish). Operated the city's first Black Catholic high school (to 1967); governance by Archdiocese/parish and women religious, not Black lay governance.

name: Saturday morning cleaning ritual
description: Intensive Saturday house-cleaning in Black households: deep-cleaning every room, all-day laundry with Sunday clothes inspected and pressed, strategic grocery shopping, cooking ahead for the week (beans, rice, fried chicken, greens for Sunday dinner), yard and porch work, and laying out pressed Sunday outfits with polished shoes on Saturday evening — in preparation for Sunday church. Ethnographic research ties the practice to cultural tradition and respectability; it persists in cultural memory and in households that keep it.

name: Search for Missing Persons (radio program)
description: A 1938 Jack L. Cooper radio program on WSBC Chicago dedicated to reuniting Black listeners with family members and friends separated by migration, incarceration, or economic hardship — one of the earliest uses of radio as social service in the Black community. Cooper, the first African American radio announcer/DJ (The All-Negro Hour debuted Nov 3, 1929), built the program into his Black-oriented WSBC lineup; by 1947 his company controlled ~40 hours/week on four Chicago stations.

name: Sunday dinner
description: The elaborate post-church Sunday meal — fried chicken, macaroni and cheese, collard greens, sweet potato pie — as a weekly family gathering for storytelling, gossip, memory-making, and transmitting cooking traditions.

name: Soul food cooking in migration-era Chicago
description: Southern culinary traditions carried north in the Great Migration — fried chicken and fish, barbecue, chitterlings, souse, greens, cornbread — first stigmatized by the Black middle class, later embraced as racial identity; adapted to urban kitchens, hot plates, and eventually canned/frozen foods.

name: Studs Terkel Radio Archive (WFMT)
description: Decades of WFMT radio interviews by oral historian Studs Terkel with ordinary Chicagoans; includes the Terkel-Charlemae Rollins 'Christmas Gif'' broadcast and interviews across Hard Times, Division Street, and Working.

name: Sunday cruising and car culture on the South Side
aliases: Sunday cruisin'; South Side car culture
description: Cars as display, status, and social life: dressed-up evening cruising and the practice of "gawking and being gawked at" on commercial strips; modern continuation in Chicago lowrider shows and cruising culture.

name: Summering at Idlewild, Michigan — the Black vacation circuit
description: Black Chicago families driving to Idlewild, Michigan ("the Black Eden"), founded 1912, where Black families could own property and vacation free from humiliation; peak 1950s, up to 25,000 visitors per summer season, with nightclub performances by major Black entertainers.

name: Soul food restaurants and the Sunday-dinner economy
description: Black-owned soul food restaurants as everyday and Sunday institutions — multi-generational family operations serving smothered pork chops, fried chicken, catfish, greens, mac and cheese — and the practice of eating out after church. Family ownership across generations; resilience through debt and neighborhood change.

name: Sunday-morning gospel television viewing ('church before church')
aliases: church before church; Jubilee Showcase viewing tradition
description: Watching Black gospel music television on Sunday mornings as a household ritual preceding or substituting for church attendance.

name: Sunday church attendance as weekly lived practice
description: The all-day Sunday rhythm — Sunday school, morning worship, dinner, evening service — across mainline, Pentecostal, and storefront churches; the week's social and spiritual anchor.

name: Signifying (ritual verbal play)
description: The Black rhetorical practice of indirect, ironic, often humorous verbal sparring — documented both in sociolinguistics and in Chicago porch recollection.

name: Soft Sheen Products, Inc.
description: Edward and Bettiann Gardner's Chicago hair-care company (founded 1964; Care Free Curl, Wave Nouveau, Optimum Care); acquired 66% of London's Dyke and Dryden (1987); merged with Carson Products (1988); Black Enterprise Company of the Year (1989); the Gardners' capital revived the Avalon as the New Regal Theater (1987); sold to L'Oreal (1998) at ~$95M 1997 sales. Terri Gardner president 1996-2001.

name: State Street / South Parkway Black business corridor
description: BVM-005 established that State Street (especially 35th-39th) concentrated Black-owned and Black-financed development, while the Regal/Savoy/South Center complex at 47th and South Parkway was principally white-developed and financed until S.B. Fuller bought the Regal in 1961. W4 encodes this distinction as the ownership-pattern anchor of Black commercial geography.

name: Street-level micro-enterprise (balloon vendor, 47th St.; newsstand, West Side)
description: Documented instances of Black street vending as business entry: a Black balloon salesman photographed on 47th Street and a Black newsstand operator on the West Side, both documented in 1970s National Archives photography. The archive caption notes that many Black business owners started with small operations such as the balloon stand.

name: Storefront Church Phenomenon (Black Chicago)
description: The dominant form of Black religious organization in migration-era Chicago: small congregations meeting in rented commercial spaces, led by minimally credentialed clergy, serving Southern migrants alienated from old-line churches.

name: South Bend, Indiana
description: Notre Dame; Freeman's professional base since 2021

name: Sheila Maxey
description: Director of CultureTechLens NFP.

name: State of Illinois
description: U.S. state; CultureTechLens NFP is incorporated as an Illinois domestic not-for-profit corporation (File #75228759).

name: St. Clara Parish
description: Roman Catholic parish at 6401 S. Woodlawn Ave., Woodlawn, founded as St. Clara in 1894. Renamed St. Clara–St. Cyril in 1969. First link in the succession chain ending at the Shrine of Christ the King.

name: St. Clara–St. Cyril Parish
description: Roman Catholic parish at 6401 S. Woodlawn Ave., Woodlawn, named St. Clara–St. Cyril from 1969 to 1990, when it was renamed St. Gelasius. Middle link in the succession chain ending at the Shrine of Christ the King.

name: St. Gelasius Parish
description: Roman Catholic parish at 6401 S. Woodlawn Ave., Woodlawn, named St. Gelasius from 1990 until the parish closed in 2002. Final parish name before the Shrine of Christ the King era.

name: St. Thomas' African Episcopal Church
description: Historic Black Episcopal congregation in Philadelphia founded by Absalom Jones in 1794; first Black Episcopal church in the United States.

name: Samuel E. Cornish
description: Presbyterian minister and journalist; co-founder of Freedom's Journal (1827), the first Black-owned and operated newspaper in the United States.

name: Southampton County, Virginia
description: Rural Virginia county where Nat Turner was born and where he led the 1831 rebellion.

name: Sojourner Truth
description: Abolitionist and women’s-rights orator born Isabella Baumfree; delivered “Ain’t I a Woman?” (1851); dictated the Narrative of Sojourner Truth (1850); met President Lincoln in 1864.

name: Southern Horrors: Lynch Law in All Its Phases
description: 1892 investigative pamphlet by Ida B. Wells documenting lynching in the American South.

name: So So Def Recordings
description: Label founded by Jermaine Dupri; Da Brat's label for "Funkdafied" (1994).

name: Solid Gold
description: Sound system established in Chicago by Jamaican producer Clifton Dillon; Chicago International Reggae Award, Best Discotheque.

name: Sam Taylor
description: Founder of Taylor Electric Company (1922), Chicago's first Black-owned construction company. Came to Chicago from the coal mines of Alabama during the Great Migration with a sixth-grade education; worked stoking coal for a railroad, running a saloon, and sweeping floors at Cuneo Press before learning the electrical trade helping Black electrician Robert Patterson at the Pullman Company. Licensed as an electrician in 1922; fought for Black electricians' union rights in segregated 1930s Chicago. Stepfather and mentor to Charles Stewart III, the first African American admitted to Greer College.

name: Symphony Center expansion completed (1997)
description: Completion of the $110 million renovation and expansion of Orchestra Hall, creating Symphony Center (plans approved June 1993).

name: Southwest Organizing Project
description: Broad-based community organizing coalition formed in 1996 in Southwest Chicago (Chicago Lawn, Gage Park, West Englewood); parent organization of the SWOP Reclaiming Project.

name: Salikoko S. Mufwene
description: Linguist; Distinguished Service Professor at the University of Chicago; scholar of creole languages, language evolution, and African American English; co-editor of African-American English: Structure, History and Use (1998).

name: Southern Illinois University
description: Public research university in Illinois (Carbondale/Edwardsville campuses). Katherine Dunham served as artist-in-residence at Carbondale (1964-1965) and joined the Edwardsville faculty in 1967.

name: SaveMoneySaveLife
description: Chicago foundation founded by Vic Mensa funding three programs centered on health and the arts.

name: Starbucks
description: American coffeehouse corporation. Mellody Hobson became its chair in 2021 (first Black woman to chair an S&P 500 company) through August 2024; Magic Johnson Enterprises partnered with it on 125 urban stores.

name: Second Line / jazz funeral influence in Chicago
aliases: Second lining in Chicago; Chicago jazz funerals
description: The New Orleans second-line and jazz-funeral tradition as carried into Chicago: brass-band processions, second-lining dance, and their influence on the city's Black musical and civic life.

name: Shelter (house club)
description: Chicago underground house/loft-scene nightclub that opened in 1990 and legitimized the city's post-Warehouse party circuit; distinct from New York's Club Shelter.

name: Sister Rosetta Tharpe — Chicago connections
aliases: Rosetta Nubin; Little Rosetta Nubin; Sister Rosetta Tharpe
description: Gospel-blues guitarist and singer (1915–1973) whose Chicago years — settling in the city in the 1920s, performing at Roberts Temple COGIC on 40th Street — shaped the 'Godmother of Rock and Roll.'

name: Social clubs and Elks/Prince Hall networks — Black Chicago
aliases: Black fraternal networks Chicago; IBPOEW and Prince Hall Chicago
description: Black fraternal and mutual-aid networks in Chicago — the Improved Benevolent Protective Order of Elks of the World and Prince Hall Freemasonry — as engines of Black civic, economic, and social life.

name: Soul Train — Chicago roots
aliases: Soul Train Chicago years; Soul Train WCIU era
description: The Chicago origins of Soul Train: Don Cornelius's 1970 WCIU-TV local show, filmed at the Chicago Board of Trade building, before national syndication moved it to Los Angeles in 1971.

name: South Side Irish parade / St. Patrick's Day — Black Chicago
aliases: South Side Irish Parade; South Side St. Patrick's Day Parade
description: The South Side Irish St. Patrick's Day Parade (founded 1979, Western Avenue 103rd–115th) and its intersections with Black Chicago: route, leadership, Black-owned businesses, and civic honors.

name: South Side community festivals (overview)
aliases: Black Chicago festival tradition; South Side festival circuit
description: Overview of the South Side's Black community-festival tradition: the Bud Billiken Parade, the African/Caribbean International Festival of Life, the Chicago Gospel Music Festival, and the city's house-music festivals.

name: Spertus Institute Black Jewish collections
description: The Spertus Institute for Jewish Learning and Leadership's Chicago archive — ~15,000 objects and 500,000 documents including the Chicago Jewish Archives — as a repository for Black Jewish history in the city.

name: Saturday night fish fry
description: The communal Black food tradition of frying fish on Saturday nights — rooted in enslaved people's Saturday gatherings, carried north in the Great Migration, and continued as church fundraisers and neighborhood cookouts.

name: St. Edmund's Episcopal Church
aliases: Church of St. Edmund, King and Martyr; St. Edmund, King and Martyr
description: Predominantly Black Episcopal parish at 6105 S. Michigan Avenue, Chicago (Washington Park). Began 1905 as the Washington Park Mission; admitted as a parish with charter filed October 12, 1940. One of Chicago's oldest active Black Episcopalian congregations; its archives (1930-2002) are held in the CPL Vivian G. Harsh Research Collection.

name: Sundown towns - Chicago-area
description: The pattern of racial exclusion in Chicago-area suburbs and Illinois towns - sundown practices, restrictive covenants, and anti-Black violence keeping Black residents out - documented by sociologist James W. Loewen. Cicero was the most infamous Chicago-area case; Kenilworth, Park Forest, and Oak Park were built or kept all-white by design or covenant.

name: Scott "Smokin" Silz
description: Original member of WBMX's Hot Mix 5 (1981); house music DJ.

name: Sam Bestvater
description: Computational social scientist at the Pew Research Center. Led the analysis behind the Center's 2023 report on ten years of #BlackLivesMatter on Twitter, finding about one-third of 2013–2021 tweets no longer accessible; noted social platforms "weren't really designed to be cultural archives."

name: Scott 'Smokin' Silz
description: Chicago DJ; founding member of the Hot Mix 5 on WBMX 102.7 FM; asked to leave the group in 1984 and replaced by Julian Perez.

name: Southeastern Louisiana University
description: Public university in Hammond, Louisiana; home of the Center for Southeast Louisiana Studies.

name: SocialWorks
description: Chicago nonprofit founded by Chance the Rapper (2016) supporting youth through education, the arts, and civic engagement.

name: Southeastern Louisiana University Archives and Special Collections
description: The archival repository maintained by the Center for Southeast Louisiana Studies, holding ~600 regional collections.

name: Subterranean Playhouse
description: DJ Slugo's record label, a sublabel of Dance Mania Records on which Slugo decided the music while Dance Mania's Ray Barney handled distribution; released DJ Slugo Presents DJ Clent: Hail Mary (SP104, 1996).

name: Samuel A. Floyd Jr.

name: Soul Food Sunday Dinner
description: Soul Food Sunday Dinner is recorded in the CultureTechLens graph as a Practice, Provisional, under project LIFE-001, sourced to CTL Thin Brief CTL-TB-000023, 'Soul Food: The Sunday Table' (2026-10-09). The brief defines soul food as the Southern-rooted cuisine — greens, black-eyed peas, fried chicken, cornbread — carried north by the Great Migration. The Sunday dinner table gathered extended family around recipes passed down through generations, and recipes and cooking techniques were passed down orally, making the kitchen a site of cultural transmission. The brief describes the meal as both nourishment and memory: a weekly practice of cultural continuity. It also records that Black-owned soul food restaurants on the South Side extended the home table into public, commercial life. Every claim in the brief is graded PROVISIONAL.

name: Step Show
description: Step Show is recorded in the CultureTechLens graph as a Practice (dance), Provisional, under project LIFE-001, sourced to CTL Thin Brief CTL-TB-000046, 'Step Shows' (2026-10-09). The brief states that step shows turn the body into a drum: stomping, clapping, and chanting in unison, staging the discipline, rivalry, and pride of Black fraternity and sorority life — claims graded SUPPORTED. Step shows are rooted in historically Black fraternities and sororities — the Divine Nine — where stepping is a signature organizational tradition; stepping uses the body as percussion, in synchronized stomps, claps, and chants performed in precise formation. The brief further records, at PROVISIONAL grade, that step shows are a staple of HBCU homecomings and yard culture, with Chicago-area campuses hosting shows that draw alumni and community audiences.

name: Sinners (2025 film)
description: Sinners is a 2025 Southern Gothic vampire film by Ryan Coogler, set in 1932 Mississippi — in the fuller guide account, the 1932 Mississippi Delta — starring Michael B. Released by Warner Bros. in April 2025, it was made on a production budget of about $90 million and grossed $366.7 million worldwide, making it one of the highest-grossing original Black horror films in history. Coogler treats the blues as historical memory inside an original-IP blockbuster, and his reported deal included first-dollar gross participation, final cut, and ownership reverting to him in 2050.

name: Soulful Chicago Book Fair
aliases: Soulful Chicago Black History Book Fair
description: The Soulful Chicago Book Fair is a Chicago book fair celebrating Black authors and Black literature, founded by Asadah Kirkland. Reader's Digest dates its founding to 2015; press coverage documents the inaugural fair in July 2016, and Kirkland's own account says she brought it to life in 2016 — this record carries the founding as 2015, first held 2016. Organized under the Soulful Book Fair Foundation, the fair has run in multiple editions on Chicago's South Side. After no 2024 edition — a gap Kirkland attributed, in a revival appeal, to illness and lack of funding — a GoFundMe campaign supported an August 9, 2025 return, and a further edition, the Soulful Chicago Black History Book Fair, was held February 15, 2026 at Little Black Pearl with Kirkland as host. The fair maintains its own site and author-submission process and is listed on the 10times event platform, where one edition is rated 4.5 from 25 ratings (checked October 15, 2026).

name: Soulful Book Fair Foundation
aliases: The Philanthropic Soulful Book Fair Foundation
description: The Soulful Book Fair Foundation is the organizing body of record for the Soulful Chicago Book Fair, named as the fair's organiser in its 10times event listing. Kirkland-circle publicity describes it as “The Philanthropic Soulful Book Fair Foundation,” providing hundreds of Black authors, poets, and composers the opportunity to share their work, and it maintains its own site at SoulfulBookFairFoundation.org. Beyond those listings, the Foundation's governance, filings, and history are not independently documented in sources located for this packet: this record is carried at Provisional grade, and no tax-exempt status is asserted for it.

name: Smithsonian Institution
description: The Smithsonian Institution is the world's largest museum, education, and research complex, established by an act of Congress on August 10, 1846, from the bequest of British scientist James Smithson, who left his estate to the United States to found at Washington an establishment “for the increase and diffusion of knowledge.” Governed by a Board of Regents as an independent trust instrumentality, it now comprises 21 museums, research centers and libraries, and the National Zoo, holding an estimated 155 million objects and specimens. In 2019 historian Lonnie G. Bunch III, founding director of its National Museum of African American History and Culture, became its 14th Secretary — the first African American to lead the Institution. In CultureTechLens research the Smithsonian acts directly: in 1987 it exhibited Marjorie Joyner's permanent-wave machine alongside a reconstruction of her Chicago salon, and in July 2022 its National Museum of African American History and Culture became joint steward, with the Getty, of the Johnson Publishing Company photographic archive.

name: Sly & the Family Stone
description: Sly and the Family Stone was the American funk and soul band Sylvester “Sly Stone” Stewart (March 15, 1943 – June 9, 2025) formed in San Francisco in 1966, built around his siblings Freddie and Rose with Cynthia Robinson, Gregg Errico, Jerry Martini and Larry Graham. The band is widely described as one of the first major American groups with a racially integrated, mixed-gender line-up, and its psychedelic soul carried “Dance to the Music,” the number-one singles “Everyday People” and “Thank You (Falettinme Be Mice Elf Agin),” and a defining Woodstock set in 1969. The darker There’s a Riot Goin’ On (1971) and Fresh (1973) followed before the original band dissolved in 1975. The group entered the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame in 1993. Stone, who had largely withdrawn from public life, died in 2025 after a prolonged battle with COPD, his family announced.

name: Still Bill
description: Still Bill is the second studio album by Bill Withers, released in 1972 on Clarence Avant’s Sussex Records. Built around Withers’s guitar, plainspoken baritone, and a working band rather than studio gloss, it extends the approach of his 1971 debut, Just As I Am: songs written like plain advice from a friend. The album contains “Lean on Me,” his song of mutual dependence drawn from the community of his West Virginia childhood, which topped the Billboard charts in July 1972 and became one of the most covered and beloved songs in American popular music, and “Use Me,” its harder-edged companion hit. The title — the insistence that sudden success had not changed him — became Withers’s public signature, and it later named the 2009 documentary film about his life. Still Bill stands as the fullest single statement of Withers’s writing: economical, unsentimental, and built to be sung by other people for the rest of its life.

name: Siegfried Schuh
description: Siegfried Schuh was co-owner, with Robert Williams, of the Warehouse when the club relocated in 1977 from 555 W. Adams to 206 S. Jefferson Street in Chicago. The Frankie Knuckles Foundation's account, carried in the City of Chicago's 2024 dedication announcement, names Schuh alongside Williams as the owners who envisioned the relocated club as Chicago's response to New York's dance club scene and who brought Frankie Knuckles from New York as resident DJ. Beyond that ownership role, Schuh is sparsely documented in the sources consulted for this brief, and no operating or creative role is asserted here.

name: Steve Lacy
description: Steve Lacy, born Steve Thomas Lacy-Moya on May 23, 1998, in Compton, California, is an American singer-songwriter, guitarist, and producer who rose from a high-school jazz band to the center of alternative R&B. He joined the Internet in 2015, while still in school, and made his recorded debut on the band's Grammy-nominated Ego Death (2015), building a reputation for self-produced work made largely on a phone. His solo EP Steve Lacy's Demo (2017) and the viral track 'Dark Red' established his lo-fi, funk-inflected sound, and that same year he produced 'PRIDE.' for Kendrick Lamar's DAMN. His debut album Apollo XXI (2019) earned a Grammy nomination for Best Urban Contemporary Album. Signed to RCA, he released Gemini Rights on July 15, 2022; the album reached number seven on the Billboard 200, its single 'Bad Habit' spent three weeks at number one on the Hot 100, and the album won Best Progressive R&B Album at the 65th Grammy Awards in 2023, when Time also named him to the Time 100.

name: Ski Mask the Slump God
aliases: Stokeley Clevon Goulbourne; Ski; Ski Mask
description: Stokeley Clevon Goulbourne, known as Ski Mask the Slump God, is a rapper from Fort Lauderdale, Florida, recognized for a rapid, cartoon-referencing flow and his place in South Florida's SoundCloud rap explosion. Of Jamaican descent and the son of a local rapper, he met XXXTentacion in juvenile detention in 2013; after their release the two founded the collective Members Only in 2014. His 2017 mixtape You Will Regret, released through Victor Victor and Republic Records, produced the platinum single "Take a Step Back" with XXXTentacion and the gold singles "Catch Me Outside" and "BabyWipe." His debut studio album Stokeley (2018) peaked at number six on the Billboard 200 and featured Juice WRLD on "Nuketown." He was named to XXL's 2018 Freshman Class and released his second album, 11th Dimension, in 2024.

name: Shaboozey
description: Shaboozey is the stage name of Collins Obinna Chibueze (born May 9, 1995, in Woodbridge, Virginia), the Nigerian American singer whose fusion of country, hip-hop, and Americana produced the defining song of 2024. On April 12, 2024, he released 'A Bar Song (Tipsy),' built on an interpolation of J-Kwon's 2004 'Tipsy'; the single climbed to No. 1 on the Billboard Hot 100 and stayed there for nineteen weeks, tying the record set by Lil Nas X's 'Old Town Road' for the longest-running No. 1 in the chart's history. The same season, Beyoncé (CTL-E-1771) featured him twice on Cowboy Carter — on 'SPAGHETTII,' alongside Linda Martell, and on 'SWEET HONEY BUCKIIN'' — and his third album, Where I've Been, Isn't Where I'm Going, followed on May 31, 2024. At the 2025 Grammy Awards he earned five nominations without a win; at the 2026 awards he won Best Country Duo/Group Performance for 'Amen,' with Jelly Roll — the Academy's artist page totals one win against eight nominations. A Black artist tying country's biggest chart record, on a song descended from a St. Louis rap hit, is the genre's whole history in a single single.

name: Student Nonviolent Coordinating Committee (SNCC)
description: The Student Nonviolent Coordinating Committee — SNCC, pronounced 'snick' — was founded in April 1960 at Shaw University in Raleigh, North Carolina, at a conference of student sit-in leaders convened by Ella Baker (CTL-E-5393), the veteran organizer who urged the students to build an organization of their own rather than become a youth wing of an older group. SNCC became the movement's shock troops and its most democratic instrument: field secretaries who lived in the Deep South's most dangerous counties, organized voter registration where the NAACP's chapters had been crushed, sustained the Freedom Rides after the first buses burned, and built Freedom Summer and the Mississippi Freedom Democratic Party. Its chairmen included John Lewis and, from 1966, Stokely Carmichael, under whom the organization turned toward Black Power (CTL-E-5430). SNCC's wager was that local people, organized patiently, were the movement — 'strong people don't need strong leaders,' in Baker's formulation. The organization faded by the early 1970s, but its alumni carried its method into every American movement that followed.

name: Selma to Montgomery Marches (1965)
aliases: Selma Marches; Selma to Montgomery March; Bloody Sunday
description: In March 1965 the voting-rights campaign in Selma, Alabama, produced the three marches the intake timeline compresses into one stop. On March 7 — Bloody Sunday — Alabama state troopers and a county posse attacked some six hundred peaceful marchers at the Edmund Pettus Bridge as they set out for Montgomery, beating John Lewis, Hosea Williams, and dozens more on national television. A second march, led by Martin Luther King Jr. two days later, turned back at the bridge in deference to a court order; that night a white minister who had answered King's call, James Reeb, was beaten to death in Selma's streets. Under federal court protection, the third march left Selma on March 21 and walked the fifty-four miles to Montgomery, swelling to some twenty-five thousand people at the state capitol on March 25, where King delivered his 'How Long? Not Long' address. The marches converted the country: President Johnson addressed Congress for a voting-rights bill in the campaign's second week, and the Voting Rights Act (CTL-E-5429) was law by August.

name: Shirley Chisholm
description: Shirley Chisholm (born November 30, 1924, in Brooklyn, New York) was the first Black woman elected to the United States Congress, winning a Brooklyn seat in 1968 under the slogan she carried for life: 'Unbought and Unbossed.' On January 25, 1972, she announced her candidacy for the Democratic nomination for President of the United States — the stop the intake timeline files at 1972 — becoming the first Black candidate to run for a major party's presidential nomination and the first woman to seek the Democratic nomination. Shut out of primary debates and most state ballots' machinery, she campaigned anyway in a dozen primaries and arrived at the Democratic convention with roughly 152 delegates, building the coalition arithmetic — Black voters, women, the young, the poor — that later campaigns would inherit. She served seven terms in the House, co-founded the Congressional Black Caucus, and helped create the WIC food program. She died on January 1, 2005. The audit found neither Chisholm nor her campaign anywhere in the graph — only a namesake — making her one of the paste's two person-shaped holes; this record fills it.

name: Sandra Jackson-Opoku
description: Sandra Jackson-Opoku is a Chicago novelist, poet, screenwriter, and journalist whose fiction braids Chicago ground with the wider African diaspora. She has taught at Columbia College Chicago, at Chicago State University, and in special programs at the Robert Taylor Homes, and has presented at libraries, bookstores, and universities across the world. Her first novel, The River Where Blood Is Born (1997), follows one family's daughters across two centuries and three continents, from ancient Africa into contemporary America; it won the American Library Association Black Caucus Award for best fiction. Hot Johnny (and the Women Who Loved Him) (2001) became an Essence magazine bestseller. With Quraysh Ali Lansana she co-edited Revise the Psalm (2017), a centenary gathering of work celebrating Gwendolyn Brooks. Her honors include a National Endowment for the Arts fiction fellowship and a City of Chicago Esteemed Artist Award, and in 2025 she launched the Savvy Summers mystery series with Savvy Summers and the Sweet Potato Crimes.

name: St. Sabina Catholic Church
aliases: Saint Sabina Church; The Faith Community of Saint Sabina; St. Sabina Parish
description: St. Sabina Catholic Church is a parish of the Archdiocese of Chicago in Auburn Gresham, founded in July 1916 when Archbishop George W. Mundelein sent Rev. Thomas Egan to establish it; Egan celebrated the first Mass on July 9, 1916, in a storefront at 7915 South Ashland Avenue. Built up by Irish Catholic parishioners, it became one of Chicago's largest parishes, then nearly closed during the white-flight era. From 1981 its pastor has been Fr. Michael Pfleger — a white priest, appointed associate pastor in 1975 and, at thirty-one, the archdiocese's youngest pastor — under whom the predominantly African American parish was refocused into a national symbol of Black Catholic social-justice ministry, with a social service center, employment resource center, and senior housing serving Auburn Gresham from its campus at 1210 West 78th Place.

name: Shabaka
aliases: Shabaka Hutchings; Shabaka Akua Lumumba Kamau Iyapo Hutchings; King Shabaka
description: Shabaka (born Shabaka Akua Lumumba Kamau Iyapo Hutchings, 1984, in London, England) is a British jazz saxophonist, clarinettist, flutist, composer, and bandleader. Born in London and raised largely in Barbados, where he began clarinet at nine and played in calypso bands, he studied at the Guildhall School of Music and became a defining figure of the 2010s London jazz resurgence — leading Sons of Kemet, The Comet Is Coming (as King Shabaka), and Shabaka and the Ancestors, and playing with the Sun Ra Arkestra and Mulatu Astatke. After announcing a public hiatus from the saxophone from 2024, he turned to flutes drawn from many traditions. His solo records include the EP Afrikan Culture (2022), Perceive Its Beauty, Acknowledge Its Grace (2024), and Of the Earth (2026) — the subject of CTL Short #53, and the first record he produced and performed entirely by himself.

name: Shani Davis
description: Shani Davis (born August 13, 1982, in Chicago, Illinois) is an American speed skater who became the first Black athlete to win an individual gold medal at a Winter Olympics. Raised in Hyde Park on Chicago's South Side, he began roller skating at age two, switched to ice at six, and trained with the Evanston Speedskating Club; at ten he moved with his mother to Rogers Park to be nearer the rink. He won five National Age Group Championships between 1995 and 2003, became the first Black American Olympic speed skater at the 2002 Salt Lake City Games, and won the World Allround Championship in 2005 and again in 2006, while pursuing undergraduate study at Northern Michigan University in Marquette. On February 18, 2006, in Turin, he won the Olympic 1,000 meters in 1:08.89 and added silver in the 1,500 meters; in Vancouver in 2010 he repeated both results. He held world records at both distances and retired in November 2019.

name: Sasha Obama
description: Sasha Obama, born Natasha Marian Obama on June 10, 2001, in Chicago, Illinois, is the younger daughter of Barack Obama, the 44th president of the United States, and Michelle Obama. She grew up largely in the public eye, moving into the White House with her family in January 2009 at age seven and remaining there through her father's two terms, which ended in January 2017. She attended the University of Chicago Laboratory Schools and then Sidwell Friends School in Washington, D.C., graduating from Sidwell Friends in 2019. Contemporary reporting documented her plans, announced that year, to attend the University of Michigan, where she studied before transferring. In May 2023 she graduated from the University of Southern California with a sociology degree, an event attended by her parents and widely covered by national outlets. Since college she has lived in Los Angeles. Although a member of the most closely watched American family of her generation, she maintains a notably private life, with no official public office or professional role, and her public record is largely the documented milestones of her education.

name: Santita Jackson
description: Santita Jackson (born July 17, 1963, in Greensboro, North Carolina) is an American singer, political commentator, and radio and television host raised in Chicago, Illinois, the eldest daughter of civil rights leader Jesse Jackson and Jacqueline Jackson. A Whitney Young Magnet High School graduate who attended Howard University, she sang professionally from her teens, touring for more than five years as a backup singer for Roberta Flack and performing with the ensemble on Stevie Wonder's Songs in the Key of Life, and she recorded with Quincy Jones and in the band of Stephen Stills. At Operation PUSH she served as a producer and vocalist, and she was executive producer and vocalist of the Aretha Franklin–sung “(A Message From) The Lord's Prayer.” She hosted the nationally syndicated radio program “Sunday Morning Live with Santita Jackson,” distributed by Premiere Networks, and is a contributor to WVON 1690 AM, Chicago's historic Black talk station, alongside her syndicated political commentary and her work as a television commentator. Her career joins gospel-rooted musicianship to Black Chicago's civic institutions.

name: Sam Richardson
description: Sam Richardson, born January 12, 1984, in Detroit, Michigan, is an American actor, comedian, and writer, the son of a Ghanaian mother and an African-American father. His aunt, Barbara-Rose Collins, became in 1990 the first Black woman from Michigan elected to the United States Congress. Richardson graduated from the University of Detroit Jesuit High School and Academy in 2002, studied theater at Wayne State University, and trained and performed with The Second City in Detroit and then Chicago. After moving to Los Angeles he joined HBO's Veep as the guileless aide Richard Splett, becoming a series regular in the show's fourth season. He co-created and starred in Comedy Central's Detroiters (2017–2018) with Tim Robinson, led the Apple TV+ mystery-comedy The Afterparty (2022–2023), and won the 2023 Primetime Emmy Award for Outstanding Guest Actor in a Comedy Series for playing Edwin Akufo on Ted Lasso, after a nomination the previous year.

name: Stephanie Coleman
aliases: Stephanie D. Coleman; Daughter of Englewood
description: Stephanie Coleman, born Stephanie D. Coleman on April 13, 1988, in Chicago, Illinois, is the alderman of Chicago's 16th Ward, representing Englewood and surrounding South Side neighborhoods. She is the daughter of Shirley Coleman, who held the same ward's seat from 1991 to 2007, and is known by the nickname “Daughter of Englewood.” Coleman earned a bachelor's degree in business management from Robert Morris University and a master's degree in nonprofit management from the Spertus Institute, and worked as an aide to Cook County Commissioner Dennis Deer. She first ran for the seat in 2015, losing a narrow runoff to incumbent Toni Foulkes, then defeated Foulkes in the 2019 runoff with 67 percent of the vote, taking office on May 20, 2019, at age 30 — the youngest African American woman then serving on the Chicago City Council. She has served as the ward's Democratic committeeman since 2016 and, since June 2023, as chair of the Chicago Aldermanic Black Caucus.

name: Salt
description: Salt (Cheryl James) is the lead principal of Salt-N-Pepa, the Queens group that made women commercially undeniable in rap. James and Sandra "Pepa" Denton were nursing students at Queensborough Community College when James's boyfriend, producer Hurby Azor, recruited them to record in 1985. Their debut album Hot, Cool & Vicious (1986) sold more than a million copies in the United States, making Salt-N-Pepa the first female rap act to earn both gold and platinum certification; its B-side "Push It" (1987) reached the Billboard Hot 100's top twenty. Very Necessary (1993) sold more than five million copies domestically and remained the highest-selling rap album by a female act until 1998. The group won the 1995 Grammy for "None of Your Business," a Grammy Lifetime Achievement Award in 2021, and induction into the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame in 2025. Under the wave duo rule, James is minted as the billed lead; Denton and DJ Spinderella are named as further gaps. CultureTechLens profiled Salt in Short #159.

name: Sister Souljah
description: Sister Souljah (born Lisa Williamson in 1964 in the Bronx, New York) is the activist, recording artist and author whose name became a permanent term in American political language. A Rutgers graduate in American history and African studies who also studied at the University of Salamanca, she came up affiliated with Public Enemy — described as a member in scholarly accounts and as an associate in university coverage — and released her only album, 360 Degrees of Power, in 1992. That spring, remarks she made in a Washington Post interview after the Los Angeles unrest were repudiated by presidential candidate Bill Clinton at a Rainbow Coalition meeting on June 13, 1992; the calculated distancing entered the vocabulary as a "Sister Souljah moment." She answered celebrity with books: the memoir No Disrespect (1994) and the novel The Coldest Winter Ever (1999), a foundational text of modern street literature whose Midnight series she has continued since 2008. name: Shedeur Sanders
description: Shedeur Sanders (born February 7, 2002, in Tyler, Texas) is an American football quarterback whose college career, played under his father, head coach Deion Sanders, made him one of the most watched players in the sport before he reached the NFL. At Jackson State he went 23–3 as a starter across two seasons and was named the SWAC Player of the Year in 2022. At Colorado he set more than 100 school records; in 2024 he threw for 4,134 yards and 37 touchdowns and won the Big 12 Offensive Player of the Year award, second-team AP All-America honors and the Johnny Unitas Golden Arm Award. Projected by many analysts as a first-round selection, he was instead taken by the Cleveland Browns in the fifth round, 144th overall, in the 2025 NFL Draft — the slide CultureTechLens examined in Short #180. name: Sherron Collins
description: Sherron Collins, born Sherron Marlon Collins on March 18, 1987, in Chicago, Illinois, is an American former professional basketball player and coach. A multi-sport athlete at Crane High School, he was named a McDonald's All-American in 2006 and played at the University of Kansas from 2006 to 2010. With the Jayhawks he won the 2008 NCAA championship, was a consensus second-team All-American in 2009 and a consensus first-team All-American in 2010, and was named Big 12 Tournament most outstanding player in 2010; Kansas retired his No. 4 jersey. Undrafted, he played 20 games for the Charlotte Bobcats and continued in the NBA D-League, in Turkey, and with the Kansas City Tornados. Collins later coached at Free State High School in Lawrence, Kansas, and became head coach at Oak Park High School in Kansas City, Missouri, leading that program toward its first state championship.

name: Sylvia Ewing
description: Sylvia Ewing, born Sylvia Michelle Ewing on March 21, 1957, in Erie, Pennsylvania, is an American journalist, broadcaster, and communications executive based in Chicago. The daughter of gospel music producer Linwood Anthony Dennard and Louise Miller, she graduated from Erie's Technical Memorial Vocational High School in 1975 and moved to Chicago in 1977. She co-founded City Life magazine, worked in the 1980s anti-apartheid movement, and from 1991 hosted On-Target on WVON-AM. She has been a pledge host for WTTW since 1994 and a producer of Chicago Tonight since 1999, produced WBEZ's Eight Forty-Eight from 2004 to 2006, and worked on the Steppenwolf Theatre Traffic Series in 2007–08. She later served the Illinois Network of Charter Schools as deputy director and Director of External Affairs, taught as an adjunct at Columbia College Chicago, and became director of strategic communications at Elevate Energy. In 2020 she received the Illinois Humanities Public Humanities Award, shared with her daughter, the writer Eve Ewing.

name: Sean Kingston
description: Sean Kingston, born Kisean Paul Anderson on 3 February 1990 in Miami, Florida, is a Jamaican-American singer and rapper. Signed to J.R. Rotem's Beluga Heights with Koch and Epic in 2007, he topped the Hot 100 that year with his debut single "Beautiful Girls"; his self-titled debut album peaked at No. 6 on the Billboard 200. The second album Tomorrow (2009) produced the Top 5 single "Fire Burning," and he collaborated with Justin Bieber on "Eenie Meenie" (2010). Through his own Time Is Money Entertainment he signed Tory Lanez in 2010. In March 2025 he was convicted of conspiracy to commit wire fraud and four counts of wire fraud, and on 15 August 2025 he was sentenced to three and a half years in federal prison, per Associated Press reporting.

aliases: DeAndre Cortez Way; Soulja Boy Tell 'Em; Big Draco
description: Soulja Boy, born DeAndre Cortez Way on 28 July 1990 in Chicago, Illinois, and raised in Atlanta, Georgia, and Batesville, Mississippi, is an American rapper who pioneered the internet-first music career. From 2005 he posted his own recordings to SoundClick, MySpace and YouTube; signed through Collipark to Interscope, he released the debut album souljaboytellem.com (2007), which peaked at No. 4 on the Billboard 200. Its single "Crank That (Soulja Boy)" spent seven nonconsecutive weeks at No. 1 on the Hot 100, became one of the first songs to sell three million US digital downloads, and was Grammy-nominated for Best Rap Song. Follow-ups iSouljaBoyTellem (2008) and The DeAndre Way (2010) carried "Kiss Me Thru the Phone" and "Turn My Swag On," and he built his own Stacks on Deck (SODMG) label alongside.

name: Safaree Samuels
description: Safaree Samuels, born Safaree Lloyd Samuels on 4 July 1981 in Brooklyn, New York City, to Jamaican immigrant parents and raised in Canarsie, is a Jamaican-American rapper and television personality. He began in the early-2000s New York group the Hoodstars, which included Nicki Minaj, and became her hype man and collaborator, co-writing "Did It On'em" for Pink Friday (2010) and holding a co-executive producer and A&R coordinator credit on Pink Friday: Roman Reloaded (2012) in biographical accounts. After that partnership ended in 2014 he released the mixtapes It Is What It Is and its second volume (2015) and the debut studio album Straitt (2020). He joined Love & Hip Hop: Hollywood in 2016 and went on to appear in the New York, Atlanta and Miami editions as well — the only cast member in all four franchises — and won E!'s House of Villains season two in December 2024.

name: Sid McCoy
aliases: Sidney Charles McCoy; The Real McCoy
description: Sid McCoy (born Sidney Charles McCoy, October 24, 1922, in Chicago; died November 5, 2009, in Los Angeles) was a Chicago disc jockey, record producer, and television announcer. He is best documented in two lanes. In the first, he was the principal jazz producer for Chicago's Vee-Jay Records from the late 1950s into the early 1960s, producing sessions by Wayne Shorter, Wynton Kelly, Lee Morgan, and Eddie Harris. In the second, he was the longtime announcer of Soul Train, Don Cornelius's Chicago-born dance program, a role he held across the show's syndicated decades alongside acting appearances in television series of the era. Between those lanes sits his Chicago radio work, remembered by listeners as "The Real McCoy," a late-night jazz program heard first on WGES (1390 AM) and then on WCFL, where he later co-hosted with Yvonne Daniels; listener recollection, gathered in radio-history archives, credits his broadcasts with introducing a generation of Chicago-area listeners to modern jazz. The graph's WVON packet found no documented WVON affiliation for McCoy, and none is claimed on this record.

name: St. Louis Stars
aliases: St. Louis Stars (II); St. Louis Stars (1937)
description: The St. Louis Stars of this record were a Negro leagues baseball club from St. Louis, Missouri, formed in 1936 as an independent team that joined the newly founded Negro American League for its charter season in 1937 and disbanded before the 1938 season because of financial difficulties. The club played its home games at Metropolitan Park. Baseball-Reference's Negro American League register lists the Stars among the league's eight 1937 clubs, alongside Birmingham, Chicago, Cincinnati, Detroit, Indianapolis, Kansas City and Memphis. This Stars club was an entirely different organization from the original St. Louis Stars, the Negro National League club that played from 1922 to 1931 after replacing the St. Louis Giants, and the two are not blended in this record: the 1937 club's history begins in 1936, a half-decade after the earlier club folded with its league in 1931. The Stars name was used again in St. Louis in 1939 by another distinct club, the team that became the St. Louis–New Orleans Stars; that later reuse is likewise outside this record, which covers only the 1936–1937 organization and its single Negro American League season.

name: Stephen Curry
aliases: Wardell Stephen Curry II; Steph Curry
description: Wardell Stephen Curry II (born March 14, 1988, in Akron, Ohio) is an American professional basketball player, a point guard who has played his entire NBA career for the Golden State Warriors. At Davidson College from 2006 to 2009 he was twice named Southern Conference Player of the Year and set the all-time scoring records for both Davidson and the Southern Conference. Golden State drafted him seventh overall in 2009. With the Warriors he has won four NBA championships, in 2015, 2017, 2018 and 2022, and was named the NBA's Most Valuable Player in 2015 and 2016; the 2016 award made him the first player in league history elected MVP by a unanimous vote, in a season in which he made a record 402 three-pointers and the Warriors won a record 73 games. He was named NBA Finals MVP in 2022. Curry is the son of former NBA player Dell Curry. In 2024 he won an Olympic gold medal with the United States team in Paris, and he remains an active Warriors player entering the 2026–27 season.
