name: Salt-N-Pepa
description: Salt-N-Pepa is an American hip-hop group formed in New York City in 1985, composed of Salt (Cheryl James), Pepa (Sandra Denton) and DJ Spinderella (Deidra Roper) — each of whom already holds a record in this graph. Their debut album, Hot, Cool & Vicious (1986), sold more than one million copies in the United States, making them the first female rap act to earn both gold and platinum RIAA certification, and its single 'Push It' (1987) reached the Billboard Hot 100 top twenty. Blacks' Magic (1990) carried 'Let's Talk About Sex,' and Very Necessary (1993), with 'Shoop' and 'Whatta Man' with En Vogue, sold more than five million copies domestically and remained the highest-selling rap album by a female act until 1998. In 1995 the group won the Grammy Award for Best Rap Performance by a Duo or Group for 'None of Your Business,' a first for a female rap act. They received the Grammy Lifetime Achievement Award in 2021, a Hollywood Walk of Fame star, and induction into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame in 2025 under the Musical Influence Award, reported as the first female hip-hop act so inducted. Worldwide sales exceed fifteen million records.

name: Shahadi Wright Joseph
description: Shahadi Wright Joseph, born 29 April 2005 in New York City and raised in East New York, Brooklyn, is an American actress, singer and dancer who was performing professionally before she turned ten. Dancing from the age of two and trained at Purelements, the Brooklyn dance studio founded by her father, she made her Broadway debut as young Nala in The Lion King at nine, then joined the original Broadway cast of School of Rock as Madison. In 2016 she played Little Inez Stubbs in NBC's Hairspray Live!, and from 2018 she carried the lead role of Holiday Anders in the podcast Six Minutes. Her film breakthrough came in 2019 with a double assignment: the dual role of Zora Wilson and her Tethered double Umbrae in Jordan Peele's Us, which earned her Saturn Award and Critics' Choice Movie Award nominations, and the voice of young Nala in Disney's photorealistic remake of The Lion King, a return to the character she had first played on stage. In 2021 she took the leading role of Ruby Lee Emory in Amazon Prime Video's horror drama Them, set in 1950s Los Angeles.

name: Skai Jackson
description: Skai Jackson, born 8 April 2002 on Staten Island, New York City, is an American actress of Afro-Honduran and African-American descent who began work as a child model in national commercials. After early screen roles including the independent film Liberty Kid (2007), she became known to a generation of viewers as Zuri Ross on Disney Channel's Jessie (2011–2015), a role she carried into the spin-off Bunk'd (2015–2018) and for which she received an NAACP Image Award nomination. Time magazine included her on its list of most influential teens in 2016. She later voiced roles in the Marvel Rising franchise and DreamWorks Dragons: Rescue Riders, published the memoir Reach for the Skai in 2019, and reached the semi-finals of Dancing with the Stars in 2020.

name: Shawn Fonteno
aliases: Shawn Darnell Fonteno; Solo; OG Solo
description: Shawn Fonteno, born Shawn Darnell Fonteno on 8 April 1968 in South Los Angeles and raised in Watts, California, is an American actor and rapper also known as Solo. After early film roles in 3 Strikes (2000) and The Wash (2001) and a small voice part in Grand Theft Auto: San Andreas (2004), he was cast by Rockstar Games as Franklin Clinton, one of the three playable protagonists of Grand Theft Auto V (2013), providing both the character's voice and his motion-capture performance. GamesRadar+'s interview with Fonteno marks his return as Franklin in Grand Theft Auto Online's The Contract update (2021), alongside Dr. Dre. In 2022 he published the memoir Game Changer, recounting his path from Watts to one of the best-known roles in video-game history.

name: Sacred Ground
aliases: Sacred Ground: The Chicago Streets of Timuel Black
description: Sacred Ground: The Chicago Streets of Timuel Black is the 2019 memoir of Chicago historian, educator, and activist Timuel D. Black Jr., published by Northwestern University Press in January 2019 in a 216-page paperback edition edited by Bart Schultz with Susan Klonsky. The narrative opens in 1919, when the infant Black arrived in Chicago from Birmingham, Alabama, with his family during the first Great Migration, in the summer of the Chicago race riot. It recounts his childhood and schooling in Bronzeville and other South Side neighborhoods, his service in Europe during World War II and the conflicts Black soldiers faced, and his later work as a labor organizer, teacher, and activist alongside figures including Duke Ellington and Martin Luther King Jr. The memoir closes with reflections on his friend and mentee Barack Obama and on a lifetime of students and community work in the city he called his sacred ground.

name: Spencer Leak Jr.
description: Spencer Leak Jr. was a Chicago funeral director and vice president of Leak & Sons Funeral Homes, the Black-owned family business founded by his grandfather, the Rev. A. R. Leak, in 1933. A third-generation leader of the firm, he began working in it as a boy and, by his own account to the Chicago Sun-Times, was answering phones at twelve and serving as a funeral attendant in his teens. He earned a Bachelor of Science degree in mortuary science and funeral service at Southern Illinois University in Carbondale, became a licensed funeral director in 1989 at about twenty years old, and rose to vice president of Leak and Sons in 1993, before his twenty-fourth birthday. He led the firm alongside his father, Spencer Leak Sr., and his brothers Stacy and Stephen, and the family statement remembered him as an advocate for families who could not afford a burial and a mentor to Chicago entrepreneurs. In February 2026 he helped guide the Leak family's care for the funeral of the Rev. Jesse L. Jackson. Leak died on May 31, 2026, at age fifty-six, survived by his wife Donna and their children, Emma and Spencer Leak III.

name: Shaquille O'Neal
description: Shaquille O'Neal, born Shaquille Rashaun O'Neal on 6 March 1972 in Newark, New Jersey, is an American former professional basketball player and sports analyst, the dominant center of his era. After playing at Louisiana State University, he was selected first overall by the Orlando Magic in the 1992 NBA draft and named Rookie of the Year in 1993, leading Orlando to the 1995 NBA Finals. He signed with the Los Angeles Lakers in 1996 and, alongside Kobe Bryant, won three consecutive championships in 2000, 2001 and 2002, earning Finals Most Valuable Player honors each time and the league MVP award in 2000. Traded to the Miami Heat in 2004, he won a fourth championship in 2006. He closed his 19-year career with shorter stints in Phoenix, Cleveland and Boston, retiring in 2011 with 28,596 points and 15 All-Star selections. He was inducted into the Naismith Memorial Basketball Hall of Fame in 2016 and remains an analyst on Inside the NBA.

name: Saquon Barkley
description: Saquon Barkley, born 9 February 1997 in the Bronx, New York, is an American football running back for the Philadelphia Eagles. Raised in Pennsylvania, he starred at Penn State and was selected by the New York Giants with the second overall pick of the 2018 NFL Draft, winning NFL Offensive Rookie of the Year. After six seasons in New York he signed with Philadelphia in March 2024 and produced one of the greatest seasons ever played by a running back: 2,005 rushing yards in the regular season, making him the ninth player in NFL history to pass 2,000, plus 499 more rushing yards in the postseason. The Eagles won Super Bowl LIX over Kansas City on 9 February 2025, his 28th birthday, and Barkley was named NFL Offensive Player of the Year. Philadelphia then signed him to a two-year, $41.2 million extension that made him the first running back in NFL history to average more than $20 million per year. He remained Philadelphia's starting running back in the 2026 season, with 8,538 career rushing yards through Week 4.

name: Sengstacke Enterprises
description: Sengstacke Enterprises was the Black newspaper chain built by John H. Sengstacke around the Chicago Defender, which he took over in 1940 and from which he also founded the National Newspaper Publishers Association. From 1965 Sengstacke assembled the chain outward from Chicago: the Pittsburgh Courier was purchased and reopened as the New Pittsburgh Courier in 1967, and the Memphis Tri-State Defender and Detroit's Michigan Chronicle joined the Chicago Defender in the group. When Sengstacke died in May 1997, Sengstacke Enterprises held those four papers, and congressional tributes entered into the Record in 1997 and 2000 describe the chain as his life's structure. In 2000, Editor & Publisher reported, the board of Sengstacke Enterprises Inc. voted to auction the Defender and the three weeklies under the pressure of an estate-tax bill of roughly three million dollars. The Defender survives as the flagship of Real Times Media.

name: S. A. Cosby
description: S. A. Cosby (Shawn Andre Cosby, born August 4, 1973, Newport News, Virginia) is the Southern noir novelist who has redrawn American crime fiction around Black working-class life in the rural South. A former funeral-home worker who lives in Gloucester, Virginia, Cosby published five crime novels in six years: My Darkest Prayer (2019); Blacktop Wasteland (2020), which won the Los Angeles Times Book Prize and an Anthony Award; Razorblade Tears (2021), an Edgar Award finalist, Anthony and International Thriller Writers award winner, and Dashiell Hammett Prize winner that landed on Barack Obama's summer reading list; All the Sinners Bleed (2023), named to more than forty best-of-year lists including Obama's; and King of Ashes (2025), whose screen rights drew the Obamas' Higher Ground and Steven Spielberg's interest. He has twice won the Anthony Award for short fiction and wrote the Marvel Crime novel Truth to Power, a Luke Cage story.

name: Sidney Poitier
description: Sidney Poitier (born February 20, 1927, Miami, to Bahamian parents, and raised on Cat Island in the Bahamas; died January 6, 2022, Los Angeles, aged 94) was the actor who carried Black dignity into the American screen's center. Trained at the American Negro Theatre, he broke through in Blackboard Jungle (1955), earned the first Best Actor Oscar nomination given a Black man for The Defiant Ones (1958), and won the Academy Award for Best Actor for Lilies of the Field (the 1963 film; the award in 1964) — the first Black man, and first Bahamian, to win it. In 1967 he was the year's top box-office draw with To Sir, with Love, In the Heat of the Night, and Guess Who's Coming to Dinner. As a director he made Uptown Saturday Night (1974) and Stir Crazy (1980), then the highest-grossing film by a Black director. He received an Honorary Oscar in 2002, the Presidential Medal of Freedom in 2009, and served as the Bahamas' ambassador to Japan from 1997 to 2007.

name: Satchel Paige
description: Satchel Paige (Leroy Robert “Satchel” Paige, born July 7, 1906, Mobile, Alabama, per his birth certificate; died June 8, 1982, Kansas City) was the Negro leagues' greatest pitcher and its most famous showman, whose major-league chance came two decades late and still made history. He began in the Negro leagues in 1926–27 with the Chattanooga Black Lookouts, starred for the Birmingham Black Barons and the Kansas City Monarchs, and barnstormed the country — legend, in his own telling, sometimes sending his infielders to sit down while he struck out the side. On July 9, 1948, Cleveland signed him: at forty-two he became the oldest rookie in major-league history and the first Black pitcher in the American League, going 6–1 with a 2.48 earned run average and becoming the first Negro leagues player to pitch in a World Series, which Cleveland won. He was an All-Star with the St. Louis Browns in 1952 and 1953 and made his final major-league appearance on September 25, 1965, at fifty-nine, throwing three scoreless innings. In 1971 he became the first electee of the Hall of Fame's Negro League Committee inducted at Cooperstown.

name: Stefon Diggs
description: Stefon Diggs, born Stefon Marsean Diggs on 29 November 1993 in Gaithersburg, Maryland, is an American professional football wide receiver for the Washington Commanders. A Maryland Terrapin who stayed home for college, he was drafted by the Minnesota Vikings in the fifth round in 2015 and became a starter in Minnesota, where he caught the walk-off touchdown in the January 2018 playoff play known as the Minneapolis Miracle. Traded to Buffalo in 2020, he led the NFL in receptions and receiving yards that season, earned First-team All-Pro honors and made four straight Pro Bowls with the Bills. A 2024 trade sent him to Houston, where a torn ACL ended his season; he recovered to catch 85 passes for 1,013 yards for New England in 2025, reaching Super Bowl LX. Released by the Patriots in March 2026, he signed a one-year contract with Washington that August, a homecoming to the D.C. area, and was on the Commanders' roster — sidelined by a hamstring injury — in October 2026.

name: Sol Ruca
description: Sol Ruca, born Calyx Harmony Hampton on 26 August 1999 in Ontario, California, is an American professional wrestler signed to WWE, where she performs on Raw. Her father, musician Paul A. Hampton, is African American and her mother is white American, a mixed heritage Ruca has discussed publicly while describing how she understands her own identity. She competed in acrobatics and tumbling at the University of Oregon and signed with WWE in March 2022 with no wrestling experience, bringing a surfer presentation and the springboard Sol Snatcher finisher to NXT. There she won the Women's North American Championship in a ladder match at Stand & Deliver 2025 and the Women's Speed Championship, holding both at once. Called up to Raw in April 2026, she defeated Becky Lynch at Clash in Italy in May to win the Women's Intercontinental Championship. In October 2026 she remained an active Raw competitor, beating Lyra Valkyria in the Main Event main event on 14 October.

name: Shakur Stevenson
description: Shakur Stevenson (born Ash-Shakur Nafi-Shahid Stevenson on 28 June 1997 in Newark, New Jersey) is an American professional boxer whose defensive mastery has carried him to world championships in four weight divisions without a defeat. He represented the United States at the 2016 Rio Olympics, winning the bantamweight silver medal, and turned professional the following year. He won his first world title, the WBO featherweight belt, against Joet Gonzalez in October 2019, took the WBO super featherweight title from Jamel Herring in 2021 and unified that division against Óscar Valdez in 2022. In November 2023 he won the vacant WBC lightweight title to become a three-division champion. On 31 January 2026 at Madison Square Garden he rose to junior welterweight and dominated Teófimo López, winning the WBO and Ring titles by unanimous decision, 119-109 on all three cards; days later the WBC stripped him of its lightweight title after he declined its sanctioning terms at 135 pounds. In July 2026 he signed a multi-fight promotional deal with Zuffa Boxing.

name: Southern University
aliases: Southern University and A&M College; Southern University and Agricultural and Mechanical College; SUBR; SU
description: Southern University and A&M College is a public, historically Black land-grant university in Baton Rouge, Louisiana, and the flagship institution of the Southern University System. The university's own history describes it as founded in 1880 in New Orleans, the first public higher-education institution in Louisiana for Black people. Black political leaders including P. B. S. Pinchback had proposed such a school at the 1879 state constitutional convention, and the legislature chartered Southern University for Colored Students in 1880; it opened on March 7, 1881, with twelve students. Designated a land-grant college in 1890, it added an agricultural and mechanical department and took its present name. In 1914 it relocated to the Scott's Bluff site overlooking the Mississippi River in what is now Baton Rouge, with Joseph Samuel Clark as its first president there. The Baton Rouge campus covers 512 acres, its thirteen teams compete as the Jaguars in the Southwestern Athletic Conference, and its marching band, the Human Jukebox, has represented the university since 1947. Southern attained Carnegie R2 doctoral-university status in 2021, the first HBCU in Louisiana so classified.

name: Stax Records
description: Stax Records was the Memphis label that built Southern soul. Jim Stewart, a country fiddle player and banker, founded the company as Satellite Records in Memphis in 1957; his sister Estelle Axton mortgaged her home to invest, and in 1961 the label took the name Stax — from the first two letters of Stewart and Axton — after another label proved to hold the Satellite name. Working from a converted movie theater on East McLemore Avenue, with Axton's record shop testing records on neighborhood youth, Stax developed an integrated house-band sound behind Booker T. and the M.G.'s and the Memphis Horns. Its roster defined 1960s soul: Otis Redding, Sam and Dave, Carla and Rufus Thomas, and later Isaac Hayes and the Staple Singers. Redding's death in a 1967 plane crash closed the label's first era; a second, Al Bell-led era peaked with the 1972 Wattstax concert. Forced into bankruptcy, the original company was closed by court order in the mid-1970s. The catalog later passed to Concord, which revived the imprint, and the Memphis site is now home to the Stax Museum and the Stax Music Academy, founded in 2000.

name: Sugar Ray Leonard
description: Ray Charles Leonard, born 17 May 1956 in Wilmington, North Carolina, and raised in Palmer Park, Maryland, is an American former professional boxer known worldwide as Sugar Ray Leonard. He won a light welterweight gold medal at the 1976 Montreal Olympics and turned professional in 1977, becoming the defining non-heavyweight star of the following decade. Leonard won world titles in five weight classes, from welterweight to light heavyweight, and was the undisputed welterweight champion. As the central figure of the Four Kings era, he defeated Wilfred Benítez, Roberto Durán, Thomas Hearns and, in a celebrated 1987 comeback after nearly three years away, Marvelous Marvin Hagler for the middleweight title. Eye injuries and retirements repeatedly interrupted his career, and he fought for the last time in 1997, finishing 36-3-1 with 25 knockouts. Inducted into the International Boxing Hall of Fame in 1997, he remains a broadcaster, speaker and public figure, giving an extended interview in October 2026.

name: Sugar Ray Robinson
description: Walker Smith Jr., born 3 May 1921 and raised in Harlem, New York, was the American professional boxer known as Sugar Ray Robinson, the fighter for whom the pound-for-pound ranking was effectively created. He turned professional in 1940, won the world welterweight title in 1946 and held it until 1951, then took the world middleweight title from Jake LaMotta in their sixth meeting. Across a twenty-five-year career he won the middleweight championship five times, a divisional record first, fighting 200 professional bouts and finishing with 173 wins, 108 by knockout, against 19 losses and 6 draws. His speed, combination punching and footwork set the technical standard later champions studied, and his Harlem celebrity, businesses and entourage made him a template for the modern sports star. Robinson retired in 1965, was inducted into the International Boxing Hall of Fame in 1990, and died in California on 12 April 1989, aged sixty-seven.

name: Simone Biles
aliases: Simone Arianne Biles; Simone Biles Owens
description: Simone Biles, born 14 March 1997 in Columbus, Ohio and based in Houston, Texas, is an American artistic gymnast and the most decorated gymnast in history. Across three Olympic Games she has won 11 medals — seven gold, two silver and two bronze. At Rio 2016 she took four golds (team, all-around, vault and floor exercise) and a balance beam bronze. At Tokyo 2020 she withdrew from several events with the “twisties,” a loss of spatial orientation in the air, yet still won team silver and balance beam bronze, and her public prioritising of mental health reshaped the sport's conversation about athlete welfare. At Paris 2024 she returned to win team, all-around and vault gold and floor exercise silver. She also holds 30 World Championship medals, 23 of them gold, and in 2021 became the first woman to land the Yurchenko double pike vault in competition. She has not competed since Paris and has not retired; in September 2026 she told the Associated Press her decision on the Los Angeles 2028 Games was still “in the works.”

name: Suge Knight
aliases: Marion Hugh Knight Jr.; Marion Knight
description: Marion Hugh Knight Jr., known as Suge Knight, born 19 April 1965 in Compton, California, is an American former record executive, the co-founder and former chief executive of Death Row Records, the Los Angeles label that carried gangsta rap to mass commercial success in the 1990s. A former UNLV defensive end who played briefly for the Los Angeles Rams as a replacement player during the 1987 NFL strike, he co-founded Death Row in 1991; its first two album releases, Dr. Dre's The Chronic (1992) and Snoop Dogg's Doggystyle (1993), defined the era. In October 1995 he posted Tupac Shakur's $1.4 million bail and signed him to the label, which released Shakur's All Eyez on Me in 1996; Knight was driving the car in which Shakur was fatally shot in Las Vegas that September. The label declined and was sold out of bankruptcy in 2009. In September 2018 Knight pleaded no contest to voluntary manslaughter in a fatal 2015 hit-and-run and was sentenced to 28 years in prison; he remains incarcerated in California, and in 2026 he declined from prison to testify in the trial arising from Shakur's killing.

name: Serena Williams
description: Serena Jameka Williams, born September 26, 1981, in Saginaw, Michigan, and raised in Compton, California, is an American tennis player who revolutionized the women's game with her power and won twenty-three Grand Slam singles titles, the most by any woman in the Open Era. Coached by her parents, Richard Williams and Oracene Price, alongside her elder sister Venus, she turned professional in 1995 and won her first major, the U.S. Open, in 1999 at seventeen. She held all four major singles titles at once twice, in 2002-2003 and again in 2014-2015, completed a career Golden Slam in singles and doubles, and won four Olympic gold medals. The WTA credits her with seventy-three singles titles, 319 weeks at world number one, and fourteen Grand Slam doubles titles with Venus. She passed Steffi Graf's Open Era record with her twenty-third major at the 2017 Australian Open. After stepping away following the 2022 U.S. Open, she returned to professional tennis in June 2026 at the Queen's Club Championships and Wimbledon.

name: Space Is the Place
description: Space Is the Place is a dual-form work: a 1974 Afrofuturist science fiction film, treated here as the primary form, and a same-titled 1973 Sun Ra album on Blue Thumb Records, covered inside this record. The film was made in 1972 and released in November 1974, directed by John Coney, written by Sun Ra and Joshua Smith, produced by Jim Newman, and featuring Sun Ra and his Arkestra, with music by Sun Ra. The Criterion Channel describes Sun Ra bringing his pioneering Afrofuturist vision to the screen in a film version of his concept album, in which Ra and his Arkestra lead an intergalactic movement to resettle the Black race on a utopian space colony, in a whirl of science fiction, social commentary, pseudo-blaxploitation stylistics, and concert performance. The film draws in part on a course Sun Ra taught at the University of California, Berkeley, in 1971, titled "The Black Man in the Cosmos." Two cuts are documented: an abridged version associated with Sun Ra at sixty-four minutes, and an uncut version at eighty-two minutes first made available in 2003.

name: Shannon Sharpe
description: Shannon Sharpe is a former professional football tight end and broadcaster. The Denver Broncos selected him out of Savannah State in the seventh round of the 1990 NFL Draft. He retired fourteen seasons later as the all-time leader in catches, yards and touchdowns by a tight end, with final career numbers of 815 receptions for 10,060 yards and 62 touchdowns in 204 regular-season games. He earned eight Pro Bowl selections and was named first-team All-Pro four times, in 1993, 1996, 1997 and 1998, and to the NFL All-Decade Team of the 1990s. He was the starting tight end in Denver's back-to-back Super Bowl titles, XXXII and XXXIII, and in the Baltimore Ravens' Super Bowl XXXV victory, after two seasons with Baltimore between his Denver tenures. In 2001 he surpassed Ozzie Newsome to become the NFL record holder for receptions and receiving yards by a tight end. After retirement he worked as a television analyst, co-hosted Skip and Shannon: Undisputed from 2016 to 2023, and joined ESPN's First Take in 2023. He hosts the podcasts Club Shay Shay and Nightcap. ESPN parted ways with Sharpe in July 2025, and he continued hosting his podcasts thereafter.

name: St. Louis Jimmy Oden
aliases: James Burke Oden; St. Louis Jimmy
description: St. Louis Jimmy Oden, born James Burke Oden on June 26, 1903, in Nashville, Tennessee, was an American blues pianist, singer and songwriter. He moved to St. Louis in 1917, performed there and took his nickname from that city, developing his work alongside fellow pianist Roosevelt Sykes. He and Sykes moved to Chicago in the early 1930s — sources differ on the exact year — and Chicago became his home for a performing and recording career that lasted four decades. His best-known record is the 1941 Bluebird release 'Goin' Down Slow,' described by All About Jazz as a big blues hit and an enduring blues classic covered countless times. His most sustained success came as a postwar Chicago songwriter, supplying songs to artists including Muddy Waters, Little Walter and Otis Spann; Waters recorded his 'Take the Bitter with the Sweet' and 'Soon Forgotten.' In 1948 he released 'Florida Hurricane' on Aristocrat Records with Waters on guitar and Sunnyland Slim on piano, and in 1949 he partnered with Joe Brown to form J.O.B. Records. A 1957 car crash reduced his performing. He died December 30, 1977, in Chicago.

name: Serena Page
description: Serena Page, born 19 September 1999 in Houston, Texas, is an American media planner and reality television personality. She graduated from the University of Texas at San Antonio in May 2022 and moved to Los Angeles, where she worked as a media planner. In college she ran a braiding business for four years, experience she later said she wanted to build into a haircare line for Black women in college. In June 2024 she entered the villa on the sixth season of Peacock's Love Island USA and, coupled with Kordell Beckham, won the season in the 21 July finale, splitting a $100,000 prize. The season became Peacock's most-watched reality series. She returned for the spin-off Love Island: Beyond the Villa, spoke at Northwestern University's State of the Black Union in May 2026, and attended the 2026 BET Awards with Beckham in June 2026.

name: Silky
description: Silky, born Jerry Woo on 21 October 1997 in New York City, is an American Twitch streamer and content creator. He began streaming in 2020, first with NBA 2K gameplay and then with Grand Theft Auto V and Just Chatting broadcasts, building an audience through interactive streams and collaborations with a regular group of friends. By February 2025 his Twitch channel had about 730,000 followers and his YouTube channel about 260,000 subscribers. In April 2024 he joined FaZe Clan as the second signing of the organization's reboot, announced on 29 April 2024, when he had more than 441,000 Twitch followers. He left FaZe Clan in the organization's December 2025 exodus of creators. In 2026 he became a founding member of CORE, an independent streaming collective formed by former FaZe Clan creators, and he was still streaming regularly on Twitch in October 2026, with streams recorded that month.

name: Schorling's Park
aliases: Schorling Park; South Side Park; White Sox Park; 39th Street Grounds; Cole's Park; American Giants Park; Cole's American Giants Park
description: Schorling's Park was a Chicago ballpark on 39th Street between Princeton and Wentworth Streets, at 39th and Wentworth, whose life the Society for American Baseball Research divides into a white major-league act, a Black baseball act, and a final decline. Opened as South Side Park, it hosted its first game on April 21, 1900, as the original Chicago home of Charles Comiskey's White Stockings, later the White Sox. After Comiskey moved his club north, tavern owner John Schorling leased the grounds, rebuilt the stands Comiskey had removed, and in 1911 entered partnership with Rube Foster. The Chicago American Giants played their first game there on May 13, 1911, and the park became Black baseball's Chicago home: Foster's club won Negro National League pennants in 1920, 1921, and 1922 and Negro World Series titles in 1926 and 1927 on that ground. SABR records crowds, a 1919 riot-era National Guard encampment, night baseball in 1930, and years of mixed sporting and civic use. Vandals set fire to the wooden park on December 23, 1940; it was never rebuilt, the American Giants moved to Comiskey Park for 1941 onward, and Wentworth Gardens housing was later built on the site.

name: Scott La Rock
aliases: DJ Scott La Rock; Scott Monroe Sterling; Scott Sterling
description: Scott La Rock (March 2, 1962 – August 27, 1987), born Scott Monroe Sterling in the Bronx, New York, was an American DJ and producer and a founding member of Boogie Down Productions. Raised by his mother, Carolyn Morant, he moved between Queens and the South Bronx before settling in Morris Heights. A standout student and athlete at Our Savior Lutheran High School, he DJed at Dugan's Bar while in college in Vermont. After graduating in 1984, he returned to New York, spinning records at the Broadway Repertoire Theatre while working as a social worker at the Franklin Men's Shelter. There he met Kris Parker, known as KRS-One; along with Derrick “D-Nice” Jones, they formed Boogie Down Productions. In 1987 the group released their landmark debut album, Criminal Minded, now regarded as one of the greatest hip-hop albums of all time — ranked by The Source among the “100 Best Rap Albums” and by Rolling Stone in its “500 Greatest Albums” list. La Rock's life was cut short months after the album's release: attempting to help D-Nice resolve a dispute, he was shot at the Highbridge Gardens projects in the Bronx and died at Lincoln Hospital within an hour. His death directly inspired KRS-One's Stop the Violence Movement.

name: Sheryl Underwood
description: Sheryl Patrice Underwood (born October 28, 1963, in Little Rock, Arkansas) is an American comedian, actress, and television host. She first rose to prominence as the first female finalist in the 1989 Miller Lite Comedy Search. She won the BET “Funniest Female Comedian on Comic View” award in 1994 and the BET Comedy Awards' Platinum Mic Viewers Choice Award in 2005, and she hosted BET's Comic View. Underwood holds a Bachelor of Arts degree from the University of Illinois at Chicago and master's degrees in media management and mass communication from Governors State University, and she served two years in the United States Air Force Reserve after college. In 2011 she became a co-host of the CBS talk show The Talk in its second season, replacing Leah Remini; she remained until the show ended in December 2024, becoming its longest-running co-host, and won the Daytime Emmy Award for Outstanding Entertainment Talk Show Hosts in 2017. A lifetime member of Zeta Phi Beta Sorority, Inc., which she joined in 1990, Underwood was elected the sorority's 23rd International Grand Basileus (president) at its 2008 biennial meeting. She is owner and chief executive officer of Pack Rat Productions, founder of the Pack Rat Foundation for Education, and host of Sheryl Underwood Radio.

name: Sam Lacy
description: Samuel Harold Lacy was a sportswriter whose columns campaigned for the integration of Major League Baseball. Raised in Washington, D.C., he began in journalism at the Washington Tribune, with a later stop at the Chicago Defender, before joining the Baltimore Afro-American, where he served as sports editor and columnist for more than five decades. From the late 1930s he pressed baseball's segregated order in print, and he is credited, with Pittsburgh Courier writer Wendell Smith, with facilitating the integration that brought Jackie Robinson to the Brooklyn Dodgers. He covered Robinson's rookie season in 1947 despite being barred from press boxes and segregated facilities, and became the first Black sportswriter admitted to the Baseball Writers' Association of America. His long-running column was titled "A to Z." In 1998 he was inducted into the writers' wing of the Baseball Hall of Fame as a J. G. Taylor Spink Award recipient. He wrote his final column from a hospital bed and died May 8, 2003, at age 99.

name: Saidiya Hartman
description: Saidiya Hartman is an American scholar and writer who serves as a University Professor at Columbia University, where she teaches in the Department of English and Comparative Literature. She earned a B.A. from Wesleyan University in 1984 and a Ph.D. from Yale University in 1992. Before joining Columbia she taught in the Department of English and African American Studies at the University of California, Berkeley. Her scholarship examines slavery and its afterlife in American literature, cultural history, law, and performance, and she is known for developing the method she calls critical fabulation, which joins archival research to disciplined speculation about lives the archive records only in fragments. She is the author of three books: Scenes of Subjection: Terror, Slavery, and Self-Making in Nineteenth-Century America (1997), Lose Your Mother: A Journey Along the Atlantic Slave Route (2007), and Wayward Lives, Beautiful Experiments (2019). The last of these received the National Book Critics Circle Award for Criticism, the PEN/John Kenneth Galbraith Award for Nonfiction, the Mary Nickliss Prize, the Judy Grahn Prize, and the John Hope Franklin Prize. Hartman received a MacArthur Fellowship in 2019 and was elected to the American Academy of Arts and Sciences in 2022.

name: Scott Joplin
description: Scott Joplin was an American composer and pianist known as the king of ragtime. He was born in Texas in 1867 or 1868, near Texarkana in the account given in the Library of Congress's National Recording Registry essay, and took piano instruction as a boy, including from the German teacher Julius Weiss. He traveled the Midwest as a performer from the mid-1880s and played at the World's Columbian Exposition in Chicago in 1893. Settling in Sedalia, Missouri, in 1895, he studied music at the George R. Smith College for Negroes, and in 1899 the Sedalia publisher John Stark signed him to a royalty contract for the Maple Leaf Rag. Joplin followed Stark to St. Louis in 1900 and moved to New York City in 1907. His published piano rags, among them Maple Leaf Rag and The Entertainer, appeared from 1899 through 1909. His first opera, A Guest of Honor (1903), is lost. He published his second opera, Treemonisha, at his own expense in 1911; it received only one semipublic performance in his lifetime, was produced in Atlanta in the 1970s, and reached Broadway in 1975. Institutionalized in 1916, Joplin died in New York City on April 1, 1917. He was posthumously awarded a special Pulitzer Prize in 1976.

name: Screamin' Jay Hawkins
aliases: Jalacy Hawkins; Jalacy J. Hawkins; Jay Hawkins
description: Screamin' Jay Hawkins, born Jalacy Hawkins on July 18, 1929, in Cleveland, Ohio, was an American singer, songwriter, pianist, and actor known for a powerful, operatic vocal delivery and a macabre stage act. He studied classical piano as a child and hoped to sing opera, citing Paul Robeson as an idol, before turning to blues and rhythm and blues. His first musical break came in 1951 as pianist with guitarist Tiny Grimes, and he made his first recordings the following year. In 1956 he recorded his own song I Put a Spell on You for Columbia's Okeh imprint. Intended as a refined ballad, the released performance was screamed and theatrical, and it became his signature recording and biggest seller; it was later selected as one of the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame's 500 Songs That Shaped Rock and Roll. Disc jockey Alan Freed backed the stage gimmick that defined his act: Hawkins emerged from a coffin and performed with props including a smoking skull named Henry. He recorded for Philips in 1969 and acted in later years, including roles in Mystery Train and A Rage in Harlem. He died on February 12, 2000, in Neuilly-sur-Seine, France, aged seventy, following surgery for an aneurysm.

name: Shantel Franklin
description: Shantel Franklin is the Democratic nominee for Illinois State Representative in House District 8 in the November 2026 general election, running unopposed for the seat being vacated by Rep. La Shawn Ford; the district covers parts of Chicago's Austin neighborhood plus Oak Park, Forest Park, Brookfield and North Riverside. Southern Illinois University describes her as the first woman and youngest Democratic nominee for the district. A Southern Illinois University Carbondale political science graduate (2016) and former Alexander Lane intern in the Illinois Senate President's Office, she served six years in the Illinois Attorney General's Office in community outreach and as a legislative liaison, per her campaign. She was named to WVON's 40 Under 40 Game Changers Class of 2026.

name: Stevie Valles
description: Stevie Valles leads Chicago Votes, the nonpartisan nonprofit that empowers young Black and brown Chicagoans with political knowledge, leadership development and voter turnout, including voting access for incarcerated people. His title varies by source: 2026 releases, including a PR Newswire get-out-the-vote coalition announcement naming him a leader of the Reimagine Civics Coalition, title him Executive Director, while WVON's roster and an October 2026 event listing style him CEO; this record carries the roster's styling with the variance stated. He was named to WVON's 40 Under 40 Game Changers Class of 2026.
